title: Insurable-at-Closing: Pay-on-Closing Insurability Sheets for WUI Listings
one_liner: Listing agents order a 48-hour parcel evidence and carrier-routing sheet before a wildfire-zone home goes to market, and the seller pays a flat fee at closing only if the sale closes.
customer: Listing agents and brokerages selling wildland-urban-interface homes in Front Range and mountain markets such as the Boulder foothills, Evergreen and Conifer, Estes Park, Black Forest and the Colorado Springs foothills. Title and escrow officers are the channel, and the seller pays through the settlement statement. A licensed WUI-specialist independent agency is the placement partner.
problem: A lender will not close without a bound homeowners policy. In WUI sales the bind often fails late: the buyer's quote is declined on a score cutoff and the contract clock is running. Neither the seller's nor the buyer's agent can say in advance which carriers will write the lot. No statute helps at that point, because the new-business decline is not a nonrenewal appeal. Free homeowner appeal kits do not touch this moment.
solution: When the home is listed, the agent orders an Insurability Sheet. It is a one-page PDF and a data file with a lot condition ledger from dated imagery and lidar, a ranked list of pre-closing fixes with cost and time to complete, and a carrier route showing which carriers' models see this lot accurately and have a human exception path. The partner agency supplies indicative appetite and quotes. At contract, buyers' agents can re-run the sheet in 24 hours. The lot evidence goes to underwriters as an exception referral at carriers that read it, and away from carriers using coarse 30 m models that will decline the same lot on a raster.
why_now: Colorado WUI homeowners' rates roughly doubled in 2020-2025 (per the parent research) and carriers keep retreating, so insurance availability is now a closing risk. HB25-1182 disclosures mean sellers can now hold a score but not a plan. Cheap high-resolution archives make a 48-hour turnaround affordable. I could not verify local closing-fall-through statistics or new pre-listing tools in this pass, so check both first.
revenue_model: A $395 flat fee on the settlement statement, due only if the sale closes; $150 upfront if the agent prefers. A $75 rapid re-run for buyer-side agents. A placement technology fee or revenue share from the partner agency on policies bound (about 10-15% commission on roughly $5k premiums, renewing yearly), structured with counsel around RESPA and producer-compensation rules. At 8% of roughly 6,000 annual WUI sales in the five focus counties, that is about $0.2M in fees in year one. Expanding across the Western WUI markets lifts this to the low tens of millions.
non_obvious_insight: The same lot gets very different treatment from different carriers. The parent research cites identical Class A homes receiving discounts of 0.7%, 12% and 41%. That suggests the profitable move is routing the lot to the carrier whose model sees it correctly, and not rebutting a score. Routing needs no statutory appeal right, so it works in California, Oregon and Washington where the Colorado law does not apply. The moat is a bindability database of carrier appetite by parcel features and actual bind outcomes. Score vendors see scores, not who binds, and agents see only their own quotes.
first_30_days: Sign one Front Range WUI-specialist independent agency as the licensed placement partner. Recruit 2 title or escrow offices and 5 listing agents. Run 20 listings with the fee contingent on closing and track policy-bound-before-closing rate, days saved and deals rescued. Get a written RESPA and producer-compensation review before any fee reaches a bank account. Turn the results into one case study for brokerage sales meetings.
lineage: mutation of I1148 ('Parcel-Level Rebuttals to Wildfire Insurance Scores'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: FireRisk.ai (RiskIntel AI), DefensibleHome Wildfire Insurance Survival Kit, Defensible Space Score (AACI Group / Five Bays Insurance Agency), Road Home Exteriors 'insurance-grade verification packets'. White space: Nobody found sells imagery-based, parcel-level, insurer-format rebuttal evidence, and nobody sells an agent or HOA 'scan the whole book for likely score errors' workflow. What exists is (a) free or $99 homeowner letter and template kits with no imagery (FireRisk.ai, DefensibleHome, Defensible Space Score), (b) slow on-site certifications (IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home, Wildfire Partners), (c) contractor evidence packets sold with hardening jobs (Road Home Exteriors), and (d) carrier-side imagery scoring (Zesty, Nearmap/Betterview, Cape, Cotality, Verisk) with at most a compliance 'framework' for appeals. Specific unserved wedge: multi-date 15-50 cm imagery that shows a lot's actual condition (irrigated, gravel-scaped, recently cleared) against a 30 m coarse-layer score, formatted for Colorado's 10-day acknowledgement and 30-day decision clock, delivered to independent agents who carry many clients. Genuine caveats that shrink the gap: (1) The premise for California looks broken. AB 75's status page shows it 'held under submission' in Appropriations on 08/29/2025 and no source found shows it enacted (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB75). The CA DOI's own report reportedly says there is no formal appeal process. So the 'statutory appeal right' in CA is unverified and Colorado is the only confirmed regime. (2) Colorado HB25-1182 (signed 28 May 2025, effective 1 July 2026, https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb25-1182) requires disclosure of the score, range and a plain-language explanation of features. It does not clearly require raw model inputs (fuel class, vegetation density), and it does not require insurers to accept third-party imagery. The 'pull the disclosed model inputs' step may be thin, and DOI enforcement is only that the Commissioner may request a copy of a denied appeal. (3) Insurers can satisfy the law with a manual mitigation discount, so a score correction may not change the premium. (4) Free and $99 substitutes cap willingness to pay for $149-299 per file. (5) Zesty, Nearmap and Cotality hold the same imagery and the carrier relationships, so the durable moat is the concession database, not the imagery. | How this version avoids them: FireRisk.ai, DefensibleHome and the Defensible Space Score serve homeowners disputing an existing score and have nothing for the sale moment or for carrier routing. IBHS and Wildfire Partners are on-site programs that take weeks, and they do not fit a 30-day contract, though they could later validate a sheet. Road Home Exteriors sells evidence with hardening jobs, not before a sale. Zesty, Nearmap, Cape, Cotality and Verisk score for carriers and do not see the buyer's bind attempt. Possible new rivals are quote-at-offer tools and portals with climate scores; they quote from their own models with no lot evidence and no multi-carrier routing. I could not check for those in this pass.

title: UK Vet Price Panel for Investors and Insurers
one_liner: The first normalized, ownership-linked, time-series panel of UK vet prices, built from the price lists the CMA now forces every practice to publish, and licensed as a data feed to equity and credit investors, pet insurers and independent-practice bodies.
customer: Three payers with different budgets. (1) Buy-side and sell-side analysts and credit or private-equity funds with exposure to listed and sponsor-owned vet consolidators (CVS Group, Pets at Home/Vets4Pets, IVC Evidensia, Medivet, VetPartners, Linnaeus). (2) Pricing, claims and panel-strategy heads at UK pet insurers and their reinsurers. (3) Independent-practice trade bodies such as FIVP, which need to benchmark independents against groups. The first buyer to target is the analyst covering CVS Group, because alt-data budgets are large and the purchase decision is one person.
problem: Consolidators keep local practice brands after acquisition, so almost no one can build a clean same-practice, before-and-after price series by owner. The CMA found consolidated practices had about 5% higher claim values and 9.2% higher prices within four years, but insurers, lenders and analysts still cannot track drift by group or postcode. Insurers hold itemised claim lines but no market panel to compare them to. Investors underwrite price-led same-store growth with anecdotes. The official RCVS comparison data will not reach approved third parties until late 2027.
solution: Crawl and normalize the published price lists monthly, keeping history. The CMA order requires 36 standard items across six patient categories (216 prices per practice), written estimates over GBP 500, itemised bills, and ownership disclosure. Map each practice to its ultimate owner using the mandated ownership statements, Companies House and the RCVS register. Deliver: (a) a monthly group-level price index and same-practice change series, (b) a practice-level API with postcode reference ranges, (c) an alert feed when a group re-prices a category. Extension beyond the 36 routine items: insurers contribute itemised estimate and invoice lines above GBP 500 in exchange for a discount, which extends the panel to orthopaedics, oncology and emergency work. Apply to become an RCVS approved third party the day that channel opens, so the RCVS feed becomes an input rather than a threat. US extension later from insurer-contributed claim lines.
why_now: The CMA's final report (March 2026) became an order with RCVS undertakings accepted on 22 September 2026. Large groups' first transparency duties start 23 December 2026, and smaller practices follow through 2027. RCVS's enhanced Find a Vet is due by 22 June 2027, with business data supply later in 2027 and sharing with third parties under restrictions. That gives a 9-12 month window in which a normalized, owner-linked panel from the start of publication is the only structured source, and history cannot be back-filled later. Cheap LLM extraction handles the mess of 5,000 differently formatted price pages.
revenue_model: Data licences. Investor feed at GBP 30-60k a year. Insurer and reinsurer feed at GBP 20-50k, with a 40-50% discount for contributing itemised claim lines. Trade-body and independent-practice benchmarking at GBP 5-15k. Month-12 target of about GBP 550-600k ARR from 8 funds at 45k, 6 insurers at 30k and 3 bodies at 15k. Marginal cost is close to zero after the crawler exists. Year-2 upside comes from extending to US insurers' claim lines (US premiums grew about 19% in 2025) and to dental and specialty procedures.
non_obvious_insight: The CMA did not only mandate price disclosure. It mandated ownership disclosure, and that is the join key nobody had. A price series linked to owner is worth far more to an investor than a price list is to a pet owner, so the buyer with the deepest pocket is not the insurer or the consumer. The panel is also a cornered resource in time: every month a rival waits is history they can never buy. The parent's canonical-code thesis still holds, because regulation just created the first common procedure list and this business maps to it before anyone else. Insurers' claim lines then extend that list into severity territory that the 36 routine items cannot reach.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build crawlers for the six largest groups' price pages and 300 independents, and load the 36-item by six-category schema. Many practices already publish some prices ahead of the deadline. Days 10-20: build the ownership graph from the mandated ownership statements, Companies House and the RCVS register. Publish a free Pre-Order Baseline note on group price levels to draw inbound from analysts and journalists. Days 20-30: pitch 15 named buyers (5 analysts covering CVS Group and Pets at Home, 5 credit or PE funds with vet exposure, 5 insurer pricing heads) on a founding-subscriber annual deal at GBP 24k with a price lock and input on the index. Target 3 signed letters of intent by day 60 and the first live index the week after 23 December 2026.
lineage: mutation of I1056 ('Unbundling Edits for Pet Insurance Claims'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VetControl (Illingen, Germany), Five Sigma (Clive AI claims adjuster), Sirma (custom ML for PetsBest, now under Synchrony), FairVet. White space: Nobody I found sells a US, insurer-facing, explainable edit library (canonical line-item codes, bundling and duplicate rules, unit plausibility, reason codes) with cross-carrier benchmarks, to mid-size MGAs and TPAs.

- VetControl is the only true direct analog, and it is German, GOT-based, a services-plus-software hybrid, and shows no US customers.
- Five Sigma and Sirma classify line items for coverage, not for pricing or bundling.
- FairVet and Vet Receipt hold consumer-sourced benchmark data with no insurer-grade normalization.
- Trupanion and Lassie built in-house and are not customers.
- Verisk has standardized the policy side only.

The unserved gap is an invoice-derived, ZIP-level, procedure-level price index built from insurer claims, which no owner-upload app can match in volume. It would be joined to explainable pay/reduce/review decisions for mid-size carriers with no data science team.

Structural risk to flag. Human-health edits work because of provider contracts and CMS rules. Pet insurers have no contracts with vets and no 'global fee' concept, and they pay owners by reimbursement. Line-level reductions therefore land on policyholders as balance bills, which invites complaints and regulatory attention. I found no US insurer RFP or public spend for this. The demand evidence is indirect: cost inflation, plus vendors like VetControl selling a similar product in Germany. | How this version avoids them: FairVet and Vet Receipt are US consumer bill-upload tools with thin, crowd-sourced data and no ownership graph, and neither sells institutional time series. Vet Price Comparison (UK) is a consumer directory, and RCVS Find a Vet is by design a directory rather than a league table, arrives mid-2027 and later becomes an input. AAHA's fee reference is a US survey, not a price panel. VetControl is German invoice verification for insurers and does not do UK market panels. Verisk's pet program is US policy and rating only. Trupanion and Lassie are in-house insurers and not customers, and UK insurers could scrape themselves but lack the cross-group history, the ownership join and neutral positioning. Selling to investors avoids the parent's balance-bill and vet-fight risk entirely, and the price index never reduces a policyholder's claim.

title: Plumber Parts Ledger: Margin Recovery Plus Failure Evidence
one_liner: Give plumbing shops a free contingency audit of unbilled parts, and pay them a bounty to bag failed pipes and fittings. The invoices become the installed-base denominator that makes the failure evidence valuable to insurers and manufacturers.
customer: Plumbing, HVAC and electrical shops ($1.5-15M revenue, 5-40 techs) as the supply side. Paying buyers are regional and mutual homeowners insurers' subrogation units and subro vendors, plumbing manufacturers and private-label buyers, and later distributors.
problem: Shops leak margin on parts bought but never billed. Plumbers also throw away the failed supply line or fitting that would have made a $9k water loss recoverable, because nobody pays them the four minutes it takes to bag it. Failure counts alone are weak, since manufacturers' lawyers can dismiss them without knowing how many units were sold, installed and stayed fine.
solution: Shops forward supply-house invoices and give a field-service export. An LLM parser ties invoice lines to jobs and returns a weekly leak list, paid at 25% of recovered revenue, with no fee if nothing is found. The same app hands out tamper-evident QR bags. A 90-second phone flow captures photo in place, date code, homeowner e-signature and claim number, and a weekly courier pickup delivers chain-of-custody parts. Each bag is auto-linked to the job's SKU, install date and installer from the invoice ledger. Outputs are subrogation evidence packs, per-SKU failure-rate reports (failures per 10,000 units sold), and at-risk-address lists for proactive replacement.
why_now: Water damage is one of the top two homeowner claim categories, and insurers are squeezed enough that routine $8-15k losses are never pursued. LLM invoice parsing now works on messy supply-house PDFs and photos, which made both products cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: 25% of recovered and newly captured revenue for 12 months, converting to $199-499 per month monitoring. $75-150 per bagged part from insurers or subro vendors (of which $40-60 goes to the shop and tech), plus a 3-8% success share on recoveries. $15-60k per year failure-data licenses to manufacturers and distributors. Later, per-address replacement programs sold to insurers as loss prevention.
non_obvious_insight: The denominator only exists in the shop's invoices, and it arrives as a byproduct of margin recovery. It converts anecdotes into rates manufacturers can't wave away. It also identifies who installed which SKU at which address and when, which decides warranty windows and statute of repose. The installed-base list is the real prize: when a lot goes bad, the insurer can pay $15 to replace a braided line at every address that received it, instead of paying $9k after it bursts.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 shops through a local PHCC chapter and owner peer groups with a free 90-day audit and a free evidence kit. Turn each audit around in 48 hours with a single 'found money' number. Pay a flat $50 per bag and collect the first 50 parts with photos. Link each part to its invoice line. Take 20 case files to two regional mutual insurers and a subro vendor and sell a 100-part paid pilot.
lineage: hybrid of I0689 + I0068 (Failed-Part Bounty for Insurance Subrogation + Contingency Audit of Unbilled Plumbing Materials). Why stronger: The audit alone is a crowded, ServiceTitan-adjacent feature with thin defensibility. The bounty alone has a cold-start problem: shops have no reason to stay engaged and the data has no denominator. Together, the free audit is the near-zero-CAC hook into the same shops, the bounty gives them a second paycheck, and the joined install-and-failure ledger is a dataset neither ServiceTitan nor a forensic firm can assemble.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Donan Engineering - Loss Logistics, Envista Forensics and Rimkus (forensic engineering / property loss consulting), LeakBot, ServiceTitan and CompanyCam (plumber field software). White space: Caveat: the session's WebSearch budget ran out (200 of 200) before any search ran. This verdict rests on direct page fetches of about a dozen vendor, industry and government sites, plus two empty GitHub searches. I did not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or trade press, so I could not rule out a small funded startup doing exactly this. Run 4-6 searches before committing money. Suggested queries: 'subrogation evidence preservation plumber', 'failed part bounty', 'water loss evidence kit', and the same on Crunchbase.

What I found is a real gap in what I could reach. Evidence logistics and forensic engineering exist for engineer-assigned losses (Donan, Envista, Rimkus). Insurer-funded plumber networks exist (LeakBot). Plumber field software exists (ServiceTitan, CompanyCam). No page I read describes any of these paying or equipping the plumber to retain the failed part on routine sub-$15k water losses. The public failure data I found is weak (SaferProducts.gov). Nothing I found is a date-code and brand-level failure-rate dataset.

Unserved specifically: (1) plumber-side capture at the moment of removal, including a per-part payment. (2) A neutral custodian and evidence package for the $8-15k tier, which is below the point where a $2k engineer is dispatched. (3) A structured brand, model and date-code failure dataset from real removed parts.

The main risks are structural, not competitive. (a) The plumber often arrives before a claim exists, so the claim number and the bounty payer are unknown at bagging. (b) Mitigation contractors and insurer-dispatched vendors may reach the site first on many losses. (c) The recovery economics of small product-defect claims are unproven, so insurers may not pay $75-150 for parts they would not pursue anyway. (d) A public brand-level failure report invites manufacturer legal pushback. (e) A 'cause-of-loss statement' from a tech risks unlicensed-engineering objections. (f) I could not fetch HomeServe (403), so I cannot say whether that plumber-network incumbent already does something like this. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ServiceTitan Accounts Payable (bill inbox, 3-way matching, Manage Statements, Manage Credits, discrepancy flags), Kojo, BuildOps (Procurement and Payables), Fergus. White space: Nobody I found offers a contingency-fee, done-for-you recovery audit for trade shops. What remains unserved is the customer-side leak: parts on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or pulled from truck stock, that never reached the customer invoice, plus supplier price drift and quoted-price violations tied back to the shop's own pricebook and markup targets. Existing tools (ServiceTitan AP, Kojo, BuildOps, Ramp) are software the shop must adopt and operate, and they focus on paying suppliers correctly. Three parts are open: (1) shops on Housecall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge or Simpro, or ServiceTitan shops not using Procurement/AP, who have no PO-to-job workflow; (2) the done-for-you, no-recovery-no-fee commercial model, which no software vendor offers; (3) a cross-shop SKU price benchmark from pooled supply-house invoices. I found no evidence anyone has assembled that for residential and light-commercial trade shops. ServiceTitan's Manage Statements and Manage Credits are the closest overlap with the returns-credit and price-error pieces.

title: Cattle Lien Registry and Sale-Barn Exit Alerts
one_liner: Invert the problem: instead of counting cattle in the pasture, watch the few gates cattle must leave through. Start with consignment alerts to lenders and lien matching for auction markets, then grow into the neutral title registry for cattle.
customer: Two-sided. Lenders with cattle collateral pay first. Livestock auction markets, which carry conversion liability when they sell pledged cattle without paying the lienholder, supply the data and pay later. Wedge: one region where 8-12 markets and 10-20 lenders overlap (for example the Nebraska Sandhills, Flint Hills or northern plains), so alerts are dense enough to matter. Eventual customers are feedyards, packers, brand agencies, participation buyers and secondary-market programs.
problem: Cattle have no VIN or title. A lender's lien follows the animals to sale, but the barn's lien check is a paper or fax list of seller names plus state central-filing lists. Borrowers consign under a relative's name, a shell entity or a barn 150 miles away, and the lender finds out months later at the next inspection, or never. Markets are exposed to conversion suits and often end up paying twice, once to the seller's account and once to the lender. Counting cattle on inspection day cannot catch cattle sold the day after, or the same cattle pledged twice (the parent's fraud case, claimed and unverified, involved a $2.8M loan against 850 head).
solution: Phase 1 (sellable in 6 months), 'Consignment Alert'. The lender uploads a pledged-collateral profile per loan: legal entities, DBAs, family names, brands, counties and any tag or EID lists from chute scans or borrower spreadsheets. Markets email or upload their consignment list before sale day, as they already assemble it for clerks. Fuzzy matching on name, brand, county and tag produces an alert to the lender ('Borrower X consigned 143 steers at Y Thursday') and a prompt to the market to issue a joint-payee check. Phase 2: EID matching. Chute-side scans (the parent's product) and barn intake scans feed the registry, so alerts match animals, not just names. Phase 3: the registry becomes a title layer where pledges and releases are recorded per animal or lot and queried by feedyards, packers, brand agencies and participation buyers. Verified movement history plus pledge status then supports collateral-managed advances on bred heifers (through a licensed lending or warehouse-funded partner) as the balance-sheet extension. The registry is tag-vendor-neutral and works on visual tags and brands where EID coverage is thin.
why_now: October-November is the peak fall calf run, so a pilot sees dense consignments right now, and lender annual renewals arrive in December-February. Digital EID tags are more common after the Nov 2024 federal rule. Cheap fuzzy entity matching and LLM parsing of messy consignment sheets make a small-team registry feasible where it was not in 2019. Record cattle prices and debt-financed herd rebuilding raise the dollars at risk per lien. A fresh fraud case (claimed in the parent, unverified) is making lenders ask what happens after the inspection. The neutral registry position is open until a tag vendor or state agency takes it.
revenue_model: Lenders pay $25-50/month per monitored loan ($300-600/yr). A bank with 150 loans is $45-90K/yr, and 40 banks is roughly $2-3M recurring. Markets get free lien checks at first because they are the data supply, then a $200-500/month tier for clearance workflow (joint-check prompts, an audit trail for their liability insurer). Later a per-lot clearance fee of $0.10-0.25/head consigned, on the well over 10M head a year that pass through auctions. Phase 3 adds registry-lookup fees from packers, feedyards and participation buyers, and net interest or fee share from collateral-managed advances through a licensed partner.
non_obvious_insight: Fraud needs an exit. Herds can be hidden, borrowed for inspection day or double-counted, but cattle converted to cash pass through a handful of chokepoints: auction markets, feedyards, packers and brand-inspected private sales. Watching the exits is cheaper and harder to game than counting the pasture. The barn has legal exposure and is a willing data supplier, whereas the borrower is not. Lender pledge data is a cornered resource: once enough lenders load it, no producer-side software vendor can replicate the registry without the lenders.
first_30_days: October is the peak calf run. Sign one mid-size sale barn (offering free service plus a sale-day lien report) and three nearby lenders who already send lien notices. Build manually, with a sheet and a fuzzy-match script. The barn emails the consignment list Monday or Tuesday, we match it against lender profiles (20-50 loans to start) and send text or email alerts within hours. Log every hit, the head at stake and whether the lender already knew, for four weeks. Aim for one or two consignments a lender did not know about, and turn them into an anonymized case. In week 4 ask each lender for $300/loan/yr on a minimum of 20 loans, and ask the barn for two more barns in its trade area. Confirm with counsel how Food Security Act lien-notice rules and state central-filing systems interact with the alerts.
lineage: mutation of I0338 ('Chute-Side Cow Counts for Ag Lenders'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global / Where Food Comes From (Beef Passport), Merck Animal Health (Allflex tags/readers, Vence). White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I ran zero searches. I did direct fetches of about 15 vendor and agency pages, plus GitHub repo searches. Nothing here rules out a direct competitor. The biggest gap is that I could not identify the third-party collateral-inspection firms that lenders already pay for cattle counts, or any startup selling vet-verified herd inventory to lenders. Do not treat 'gap' as 'open'.

What the direct fetches showed: none of the herd-software, EID, tracking or verification vendors I checked advertise a lender-facing 'independent count' product. The vendors were CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/WFCF, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg and Gallagher. Merck/Vence returned 403, so I could not check it. Every one of them is a producer-side management or supply-chain tool. GitHub searches turned up no open-source lender-verification tool, only hobby herd apps.

The unserved wedge is a lender-mandated, third-party-attested herd inventory built as a covenant workflow. It would cover the vet-signed chute-side count, a portfolio dashboard, and year-over-year anomaly flags such as head count down, pregnancy rate down, or tags missing versus last year.

Structural weaknesses to be skeptical of:
- Adverse selection: 'borrower-initiated' verification means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. The product only works if lenders make it a loan condition.
- Coverage: a preg-check only counts animals brought to the chute that day, not cattle on other leases or sold or double-pledged since. It does not prove ownership or lien priority.
- Vet liability and willingness: vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit.
- Economics: $2-3/head split 50/50 leaves the vet about $1-1.50/head on top of a preg-check fee that is already several dollars.
- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature. | How this version avoids them: CattleMax, AgriWebb, Gallagher, HerdDogg, Halter and Ceres Tag are producer-side herd management or tracking tools, and none holds lender pledge data. They cannot collect it without alienating the producers who pay them. Merck/Allflex and Vence own tags but a vendor-run registry would be distrusted by rival tag vendors and lenders. IMI Global's Beef Passport ties EIDs to verification records for the supply chain, not to liens or exits. State central-filing systems and brand agencies are passive, annual or paper-based lists, so we sit on top of them and can partner. The real risks are sale-barn clerking-software vendors and state agencies adding matching. Being lender-funded and neutral, with lender pledge data as the cornered resource, is the counter.

title: GLP-1 Palate Panel for Food R&D
one_liner: A managed panel of GLP-1 users and their households that food and restaurant companies rent to test products, portions and health claims.
customer: R&D and insights teams at mid-size CPG (protein, snacks, frozen), restaurant chain menu teams, foodservice for hospitals and senior living, and supplement brands that need claim substantiation ($25-150k per study).
problem: 73% of GLP-1 users report taste changes and 70% lose joy in eating, so 'just add protein' fails. About 70% change what the household eats, and non-users adopt 30-50% of the changes, so the affected base is ~50% larger than the user count. Food companies are reformulating and launching 'GLP-1 friendly' labels on general-population panels and conflicting forecasts.
solution: Recruit and maintain a segmented panel (drug, dose, weeks on therapy, aversion profile, household makeup). Run sensory, portion and format tests plus home-use tests and 8-12 week muscle and satiety claim studies. Deliver 'aversion maps' (which textures and smells trigger nausea at which dose) and household spillover models.
why_now: Households with a GLP-1 user doubled from ~11% to 22% in under 3 years. Pills launched in 2026 broaden the base. CPG is mid-reformulation, and FTC claim scrutiny makes 'evidence-backed' labels valuable. Purchase-panel incumbents see what is bought, not why.
revenue_model: $25-150k per study, plus $40-100k/year data subscription for 'aversion map' updates.
non_obvious_insight: The 'GLP-1 consumer' is 5-6 sensory segments that shift with dose and week on therapy, not one persona. Forecasting from sales data cannot separate them, but a panel can. The picks-and-shovels of a reformulation wave are the testers, not the brands.
first_30_days: Recruit 300 panelists from subreddits and Facebook groups with a $25 incentive, verified by photo of the pharmacy label. Publish a free 'taste change' survey report for press. Cold-email 30 CPG insights leads and land a first paid pilot of about $25k.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Circana (GLP-1s and Consumer Behavior insights hub), Numerator (GLP-1 People Groups and GLP-1 Custom Analysis), The Hartman Group - 'GLP-1s: Seizing Opportunity in a New CPG Landscape', Tastewise (GLP-1 CPG Playbook, TasteGPT). White space: Limited to what I could check: I found no vendor, on the pages I fetched, that runs a managed, longitudinal panel of verified GLP-1 users segmented by drug, dose and weeks on therapy. I also found none that does physical product testing on that panel (sensory, portion and format tests, home-use tests) or maps aversions by texture and smell against dose. The players found are all survey, signal or purchase-data based: Circana and Numerator show what GLP-1 households buy, Hartman sells a one-off $10k survey report, and Tastewise sells AI trend signals. Nothing found covers household spillover modeling tied to a panel. Nothing found offers claim-substantiation studies (8-12 week muscle and satiety) for 'GLP-1 friendly' labels. Big gaps in my evidence: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so I could not run general web searches and relied on direct fetches of vendor pages. I did not check startups, YC or Crunchbase entries, sensory CROs (Sensory Spectrum showed no GLP-1 content; Tragon and Eurofins fetches failed), generic panel vendors (Cint, Toluna showed no GLP-1 content; Dynata unchecked), telehealth companies (Ro, Noom, WeightWatchers) that could monetize their own user bases, or flavor houses (Givaudan, Kerry and dsm-firmenich showed no GLP-1 content on the pages retrieved; IFF returned 403). Any of these could already offer a GLP-1 screener or a similar service, so treat the gap verdict as medium-low confidence.

title: Mixed-Lot Calf Referee With Brix Price Formulas
one_liner: An independent, photo-stamped Brix grade taken at the broker's loading dock that turns a blind mixed-dairy calf lot into a formula-priced lot, so the best dairies stop subsidizing the worst and disputes get settled by schedule, not argument.
customer: Wedge: independent calf brokers and sale-barn aggregators who assemble roughly 200-800 day 2-7 beef-on-dairy calves a week from 10-30 dairies and sell them to raisers who have no history with any of the source dairies. Start with 3-5 brokers in one dairy-dense region. Second payer: the raisers who buy those lots. Not the target: contracted dairy-to-ranch flows and integrated operators, where source reputation already does the job.
problem: Mixed-source lots are priced at a lemons discount. The buyer cannot tell which dairy's calves are good, so he pays for the average and hedges for the worst, and good dairies subsidize bad ones. Brokers eat 'adjustments' and lose a buyer after one bad lot. When calves die at the raiser, the dispute cannot be resolved: the dairy blames luck and the raiser blames the calves. A raiser can self-test for $1, but the seller will not accept the buyer's number, and the buyer will not accept the seller's, so measurement alone settles nothing. Packers already apply standardized deductions for unknown health history, so that discount is passed back upstream to brokers.
solution: 1) Two techs sample at unload or loading: every calf in lots sold as 'graded', a 20-calf random sample in standard lots. One phone frame captures ear tag, tube label and the refractometer display, timestamped and geotagged, so custody is the product. 2) Each calf is graded on the Lombard four-tier scale and the lot gets a score. 3) The lot quote carries a pre-agreed Settlement Schedule: a price add per Excellent/Good head, and an automatic per-head credit if Poor exceeds an agreed share of the lot (for example 30%). The buyer accepts or rejects at arrival by formula. This is a price term, not insurance or a warranty. 4) The broker uses the grades to split lots by dairy quality and sell the top tier at a spread. 5) The referee also holds the tag-level chain of custody for any 30-day death dispute (necropsy photo plus treatment log).
why_now: Crossbred calves at $1,000-1,500 make a 10-point mortality gap worth $100+ a head, so the number now matters to a broker's P&L. Feeders are being told not to assume a crossbred premium, so the market's question is shifting from 'what genetics' to 'which calves live'. The Lombard 2020 four-tier standard exists, digital refractometers cost about $150, and photo-stamped custody capture on a phone is now trivial to build. The same lot could not have been priced this way in 2019, when a calf was worth a fraction as much.
revenue_model: $5 per graded calf, split between broker and buyer. In the first 90 days, success-based: the fee is due only on lots that clear at least $10 a head over the ungraded quote, so grading pays for itself before it bills. Add $75 per settlement or claim adjudication and a $250/month broker dashboard with a dairy league table. Honest sizing: 300 calves a week per broker is about $78K a year, so 15 brokers is about $1.2M. Test fees alone cap out in the low millions, so the wedge's real value is the custody dataset, which is the base for the guarantee and warranty layers in the other branches.
non_obvious_insight: The product is not the number, it is the pre-agreed price formula attached to it. Disclosure unravels (Grossman-Milgrom): once the two or three best dairies in a lot prove Excellent, any dairy that refuses grading gets priced as Poor, so you only have to win the best sellers rather than the whole market. And no buyer needs to state a premium: the money is the lemons discount already being taken out of good calves in mixed lots, which sidesteps the 'no proven crossbred premium' headwind.
first_30_days: Week 1: recruit one broker or sale barn moving 300+ calves a week, and pick their 3 best dairies (the ones who want to prove it). Buy two refractometers, tubes and centrifuge or clot rack, and set up a photo-stamp capture form on a no-code tool. Weeks 2-4: grade every calf free at loading (about 1,200 calves), send lot sheets and a proposed Settlement Schedule to 2-3 buyers, and ask them to report 30-day illness and death by ear tag. Day 45 go/no-go gates: (a) at least one buyer signs a schedule with a spread of $25 or more a head between Good-or-better and Poor; (b) Poor calves show at least 1.5x the 30-day loss of Excellent/Good. If either fails, stop. Before spending on anything else, verify the 10-25% raiser-loss figure from the parent, since it is unsourced.
lineage: mutation of I0617 ('Immune-Graded Beef-on-Dairy Calves With Warranty'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Where Food Comes From (third-party verification: Age Verification, Source Verification, USDA Process Verified Program, custom Process Verified claims), Calftech Corporation (Central Valley, CA calf ranch). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I could not run the planned searches on Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or vendor names. The 'nobody does this' finding therefore rests on direct page fetches and a GitHub repository search, not full web coverage. My early attempts to pull search-engine result pages through WebFetch returned junk or CAPTCHAs, and I stopped them because they sidestep the search limit. The verdict is low-to-moderate confidence.

What I found:
- No company selling per-calf independent Brix or serum total protein grading with a QR passport, and no calf-immunity warranty product. Where Food Comes From has no such program. Vytelle's site lists no calf program. GitHub has no relevant open-source tool, only hobby repos.
- Livestock Risk Protection explicitly 'does not protect against mortality, condemnation, physical damage or disease' (https://agproud.com/articles/60060-knowledge-is-the-best-insurance-an-overview-of-livestock-risk-protection). Federal cover for calf death loss is therefore absent. I did not verify what private mortality insurance exists.

What still stands in the way, and is not competition in the strict sense:
1. Self-testing. A raiser can Brix-test at arrival for about $1, and dairies can test their own calves. Independent custody only earns money where seller and buyer distrust each other's numbers, or where price is set before arrival.
2. Bilateral history. Feeders already ask which dairy the calves came from and some supply sire straws to dairies (https://agproud.com/articles/53106-factors-to-consider-before-buying-crossbred-dairy-beef-calves). Source-dairy reputation substitutes for per-calf grading.
3. Warranty moral hazard. Immunity is one driver of loss, but raiser housing, feeding and biosecurity dominate, which makes underwriting hard. Lombard's consensus paper puts failure of passive transfer at roughly twice the risk, which is a useful signal but not a full loss model.
4. Incumbents can absorb it. Verifiers, diagnostics vendors, calf-ranch networks and packer programs could add an immunity field.

Genuinely unserved: an independent, per-calf immunity record that travels from dairy to raiser to feeder to packer, plus a neutral dispute-resolution measurement. | How this version avoids them: Where Food Comes From audits marketing claims (age, source, process) on a program basis; this sells per-lot physical sampling and a pricing formula at the moment of sale, and could give WFCF a certificate to resell as a Process Verified module instead of competing with it. Calftech-style integrated ranches keep data in-house because they own both sides; this only sells into unintegrated trade (mixed lots), and an integrated operator buying outside calves becomes a customer. The $1 self-test objection is answered because the product removes the need to trust the other party, not the need to measure. Bilateral-history substitution is avoided by targeting only lots where no history exists. Warranty moral hazard is avoided because nothing here insures the raiser's management.

title: Dual-Mode Genset Permits for Queued Campuses
one_liner: Design the air permit for new data center campuses before the generators are bought, so the backup fleet is legally curtailment-ready from day one and the fee is tied to energization date.
customer: Energy and development leads at spec developers, powered-shell builders and neocloud/colo operators with 50-400 MW campuses in PJM (AEP Ohio, Dominion, ComEd, PPL). The wedge is campuses that have filed, or are about to file, their air-permit application and have not yet placed genset purchase orders. Hyperscalers with in-house permitting teams are excluded at first. Air consultants are a secondary channel.
problem: The parent's real cost is retrofitting existing Tier 2 emergency fleets. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), emergency engines are capped at 100 hours a year, with at most 50 for non-emergency use, and none of that can earn income or serve a financial arrangement. Reclassifying an installed fleet means stricter engine standards, re-permitting and public comment. Yet the largest cohort of new engines is being permitted right now as emergency-only, because that is the cheapest and fastest path. That choice locks out capacity and curtailment use for 15 or more years. PJM's curtail-or-bring-capacity direction means those same campuses will need on-site backup to energize earlier. Nobody is designing the permit for that second use at the moment the choice is cheap.
solution: A fixed-price 'Dual-Mode Permit Package' sold before genset purchase orders and inside the air-permit comment window. (1) A one-time state legal feasibility memo from a retained air attorney (VA, OH, IL, PA), which gates every engagement. (2) An engine spec that is Tier 4 Final or SCR-ready, with catalyst and urea footprint reserved, ECM hour-metering and paralleling ready. This turns retrofit financing into a spec change costing a fraction of a retrofit. (3) Permit application language and modeling: an emergency mode plus a capped grid-emergency/curtailment mode of roughly 100-200 hours, synthetic-minor NOx limits, 1-hour NO2 dispersion modeling, and a community disclosure plan. (4) A curtailment-readiness dossier the utility and PJM can cite when offering earlier or flexible energization. Engines are certified as non-emergency-capable from the start, so the campus never has to fight the emergency-to-non-emergency reclassification.
why_now: Turbines are sold out until roughly 2029-30, so the practical path to earlier energization is on-site capacity that can be built now. PJM's July 2026 auction was 6.8 GW short, and the connect-and-manage and bring-your-own-capacity framework is being filed at FERC. Large OEM gensets with SCR options are catalog items, and campuses energizing in 2028-30 must order engines and file permits in the next 6-12 months. This would not have worked in 2019, when there was no curtailment penalty for missing on-site capacity.
revenue_model: $60-150k fixed fee per campus (feasibility memo, spec, permit drafting, modeling). A success fee applies when the permit issues with the dual-mode condition (about $50k), and a further one applies only when the utility or PJM offers earlier or flexible energization that cites the dossier, at roughly $1-2k per MW per month of acceleration. A 200 MW campus energized six months early is worth about $1-2M to us. A colo campus that size earns on the order of $30M a month at full lease-up, so the buyer's return is 50x or more. An optional 10% share of capacity revenue for five years is secondary. Illustrative unit economics: 10 campuses in year one is roughly $1.5-3M, with two lawyers, two engineers and one permit modeler.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest time to unlock diesel is before it exists. The permit design is a one-time, 15-year decision, and taking it at application costs a fraction of a retrofit. It turns the parent's hardest problem (retrofit financing plus reclassification risk) into a purchase-spec problem that the buyer is already paying for. It also changes what is being sold, from capacity revenue that the buyer discounts to time. Energization date is the metric a developer's CFO already tracks, and every month of delay costs more than any capacity payment. Public permit dockets show exactly which campuses are in the window, so lead generation is a scrape rather than cold outreach.
first_30_days: Week 1: commission the air-attorney feasibility memo ($8-10k), covering which engine and classification path works in VA, OH, IL and PA. If no path closes at Tier 4 or SCR cost, stop. Weeks 1-2: scrape VA DEQ, Ohio EPA, IEPA and PA DEP public notices for data center genset permit applications filed in the last 12 months (target 40) and identify the developer and the consultant of record for each. Weeks 2-4: cold-contact the development leads and offer a $12k 'dual-mode gap review' of the pending application inside the public comment window. In parallel, offer the applicants' air consultants a white-label subcontract for the dual-mode module. Aim for two paid gap reviews and one campus package LOI. The demand test is whether a developer will pay before PO to keep the option open.
lineage: mutation of I0836 ('Air-Permit Unlock for Idle Data Center Diesel'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Voltus, CPower, Enchanted Rock (ERock), Trinity Consultants (data center and power team). White space: Verification caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted, so no search-engine, Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or TechCrunch queries could be run. I did about 30 direct page fetches and 2 GitHub searches instead. The GitHub searches found no open-source tool for this. I found no company selling a fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' package for existing data center diesel fleets (permit modification, emissions retrofit financing, telemetry, PJM enrollment and M&V). That is absence of evidence from a constrained search, not proof that none exists.

What appears unserved:
(1) A productized, per-state permit playbook tied to capacity outcomes. Trinity-type consultants sell hourly, per-project permitting. DR aggregators (Voltus, CPower) sell enrollment and revenue share. Generator OEMs and ERock sell hardware. Nobody I found owns the seam between them.
(2) Retrofit financing on the subset of engines that need it.
(3) A permit-headroom dataset across Title V and minor-source files.

The binding constraint is legal, not competitive. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), as summarized from Cornell LII, emergency engines are limited to 100 hours a year for maintenance, testing and emergencies, with at most 50 of those for non-emergency use. The 50 hours cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, and cannot generate income or serve a financial arrangement with another entity. Only narrow exceptions exist, dispatched by local authorities for transmission and distribution limits. Selling emergency-designated diesel as PJM capacity therefore likely requires reclassifying engines as non-emergency, which triggers stricter engine standards (Tier 4 or SCR-type controls), plus state NOx limits and possible major-source permitting. That is why the founder's 'retrofit the subset' step is likely the real cost and risk. It is also why incumbents have stayed away. The wedge exists only where the permit and retrofit math actually closes.

Other risks: PJM DR accreditation rules and limited-duration derating, which I could not verify because the PJM manual fetch returned only a table of contents. Local opposition to diesel. Hyperscalers and utilities choosing gas or battery capacity instead. | How this version avoids them: Trinity-type consultancies sell reactive, hourly permit work, are not tied to capacity or energization outcomes, and do not spec engines. We offer them the dual-mode module as a white-label add-on rather than compete. Voltus and CPower can only enroll resources that are already dual-mode, so we are their upstream and never touch enrollment or the DR revenue relationship. ERock sells gas hardware and a bridge-to-grid story. We are engine-agnostic and ride on gensets the campus must buy anyway, so there is no incremental hardware capex to finance. We also avoid the parent's unproven retrofit-of-Tier-2 step and its legal trap by working only on greenfield permits, and we gate on the attorney memo.

title: Ship-Date Cliff Audits for Phased Campuses
one_liner: A fixed-fee clock-map, rider-negotiation and proof-test sprint for developers of multi-phase data center campuses whose pre-bought gensets, UPS and chillers were shipped long before the halls they serve, so the OEM 18-months-from-ship outer limit expires before startup.
customer: Wedge buyer: the VP of procurement or construction director at colo developers and neoclouds building multi-phase campuses (100MW+, with phases 2-4 not yet energized) that accepted long-lead MEP deliveries ahead of the shell. Start with generators, then UPS. Secondary buyer: the lender's technical advisor asking for an equipment warranty schedule at draw or refinancing.
problem: The judges and the competitor check both found that the parent's premise is too broad. Startup plus load-bank IST already loads most equipment, so the 'idle hall' exposure is narrow. The clean exposure is different. OEM terms run to the earlier of about 12 months from startup or 18 months from factory ship (Cummins, Eaton and Trane terms in the research). Developers buy gear in blocks for phases 2-4 to lock lead-time slots and pre-tariff prices, and take delivery into yards or spare rooms. When a phase slips, the outer limit lapses before the unit is ever started. Storage voiding conditions (heaters, battery freshening charges, engine exercise) are usually undocumented, so an OEM can also deny on those grounds. Procurement has moved on, the ship date lives in a bill of lading nobody rereads, and ops inherits the unit with no idea the clock ran out.
solution: 1) Cliff calendar. Per serial number, extract ship date (bill of lading, delivery ticket), planned startup, outer-limit date and voiding conditions. The LLM pipeline is an internal tool; the deliverable is a one-page dated list of cliffs. 2) Rider sprint. Before each cliff, negotiate a written start-date deferral or delayed-start rider with the OEM. Package it campus-wide, because the owner's phase 3-4 orders are the leverage a single-unit rider buyer lacks. 3) Storage-compliance repair. Fix missing exercise, heater and battery-charge logs so the OEM loses its easy denial grounds. 4) Proof test. For installed units 6-9 months before the cliff, run a staged load test using a load-bank rental partner, then file claims with OEM-grade evidence while the OEM is still liable. Contingency is not the lead model.
why_now: Long-lead power gear (gensets, transformers, switchgear) is being bought years ahead of buildings, and phase slippage is widespread in 2026 reporting. Tariffs make each unit more expensive, so each lapsed warranty is worth more. LLMs make serial-level extraction from delivery documents cheap. Delayed-start riders exist (Trane), so the ask is normal to OEMs but rarely made.
revenue_model: $30-60K fixed fee per campus phase for the cliff calendar plus rider negotiation. $60-120K per year campus retainer that keeps the calendar live as phases progress. Load-test pass-through with a 15% markup, plus a referral fee from the rental partner. Success fee of 20% of OEM-accepted claim value, measured by the OEM's claim number or credit memo, and 10% of the discount won on riders versus list. Assumption to validate: about 30 campus programs at roughly $80K per year is about $2.4M ARR with 2-3 people.
non_obvious_insight: The exposed population is defined by shipment date versus startup date, not by whether a hall is idle. That makes it provable from documents and public filings before any owner talks to you. It also makes the contingency-collection problem disappear: a signed deferral or an OEM credit memo is a countable outcome, unlike 'avoided repair cost'. The leverage is future orders across the campus, which the owner has and a one-off rider purchase does not.
first_30_days: Build a target list from public state air-permit filings for backup diesel generators, which typically list unit counts and models by phase, cross-referenced with press releases and county filings. Rank 40 campuses where permitted units far exceed operating ones. Email the procurement lead a one-page teaser: 'if your gensets shipped in Q3 2025, the OEM outer limit lands in Q1 2027'. Land three owners who hand over POs and delivery tickets for a free 5-day clock map. Use the first dated cliff to open a rider conversation with the OEM before any invoice. This also answers the parent's unresolved question of whether clocks are truly running out on unstarted equipment.
lineage: mutation of I0229 ('Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ethyco (data center commissioning, warranty-phase support), Anyset AI (agentic closeout / warranty tracking), Nomic (AEC document AI, closeout), Trane delayed start-up warranty (OEM rider). White space: Nobody I found combines all of these for data center MEP: (1) a serial-number-level clock ledger built for idle or deferred-start halls, (2) a pre-expiry loaded stress test using the idle capacity, (3) OEM claim filing and start-date deferral negotiation, and (4) success-fee or fixed-fee pricing sold to the owner or its lender. The pieces exist separately. Anyset and Nomic do doc extraction. Ethyco-style Cx firms do a 10-month warranty review. Wind and solar have end-of-warranty inspection and claims firms. OEMs sell delayed-start riders. Load-bank vendors have the hardware. Data center power and cooling MEP has no dedicated end-of-warranty claims specialist that I could find. (c) Documents are the commodity step, so the moat has to be inspection plus OEM leverage, not the LLM pipeline. | How this version avoids them: Ethyco and other Cx firms start their 10-month review after occupancy, so they sell to Cx and ops. title: Settlement Passports for Florida High-Rise Condos
one_liner: A satellite-radar settlement history for every Florida condo tower, sold as the cheap first page of the milestone-inspection and reserve-study file.
customer: Florida condo associations and the licensed engineers and property managers who run their milestone inspections and structural integrity reserve studies; secondary buyers are master-policy underwriters, lenders and buyers' agents doing condo diligence.
problem: Carriers want structural documents before they bind a master policy, SIRS and milestone inspections are mandatory for 3+ story buildings, and special assessments run $50K-$200K+ per unit. Boards cannot tell whether their building is stable or sinking until an engineer bills for scoping. A 2024 University of Miami InSAR study found 35 Miami Beach to Sunny Isles buildings subsiding 2-8 cm over 2016-2023, and no commercial product packages this for boards.
solution: Process free Sentinel-1 radar (2015 onward), ESA archive radar for the 1990s-2010s, and newly public NISAR L-band data into a per-building vertical-motion trend. Add differential tilt across the footprint and a comparison against neighbours built on similar fill. Deliver a 3-page Settlement Passport plus a monitoring feed, positioned as a screening indicator that sharpens inspection scope, with an engineer partner signing off. It is not a substitute for the inspection.
why_now: Florida's post-Surfside SB 4-D inspection and reserve-study mandates are now enforced and carriers demand documents. NISAR L-band data has been free through ASF since the July 20, 2026 public release, adding to the Sentinel-1 record. Peer-reviewed proof that InSAR resolves individual Miami towers exists but has not been productized. Reinsurance is softening while condo retail insurance is still squeezed.
revenue_model: $900-$2,500 per building for the initial passport and $300/yr for monitoring. Wholesale price of about $400 to engineering firms who bundle it into SIRS work. $100/building/yr portfolio contracts for management companies.
non_obvious_insight: InSAR is treated as an academic or pipeline-monitoring tool, but the buyer with a legal deadline and a real budget is a condo board that must assemble a structural file. Persistent-scatterer InSAR works best on concrete high-rises, the exact asset at issue. The 10-30 year archive can also show a building has been stable for decades, which makes it a positive underwriting asset for the many buildings that are fine, not just a warning label.
first_30_days: Run the free Sentinel-1 stack for about 400 buildings on the Miami-Dade and Broward barrier islands. Offer one free passport to each of 15 engineering firms and 5 management companies, and sign 2 engineers as resellers. Then charge the first 10 boards facing reserve-study or insurance-renewal deadlines.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Estructura (division of Dorado Services) - TerraIntel InSAR + GeoSIG sensors + GeoSMART, TRE ALTAMIRA (CLS Group; TRE Altamira Inc.), Sixense Satellite / Atlas InSAR (Vinci group), Fugro (InSAR high-rise settlement evaluation and prediction). White space: No one found sells a productized, fixed-price, board-readable per-building InSAR settlement history for Florida condo towers, wholesaled to the engineers who already write milestone and SIRS reports. The InSAR firms (TRE Altamira, Sixense, Fugro, SkyGeo, Detektia) sell quote-based enterprise projects. SatSense does per-property InSAR but for the UK. Estructura (June 2026) pitches InSAR to condos but only as one part of a sensor bundle, with no disclosed price and no report artifact. The Florida condo-data players (Domexa, CondoScan, CleanCondo, PropFusion) have no physical-movement data. Specifically unserved: (1) a $400-$2,500 report an engineer can attach to a Phase 1 milestone inspection or SIRS; (2) a 10-30 year ERS/Envisat/Sentinel-1 history that shows a building is stable, for lenders and underwriters; (3) a pre-construction baseline for a neighbouring tower's pile driving; (4) a roll-up for management companies with many buildings. A strong caveat is that this is not a technology moat. TRE Altamira already processed this exact coastline, ISCE, MintPy and StaMPS are open source, and OPERA gives a free coarse baseline. Any incumbent or Estructura could productize this quickly, so the wedge is distribution through engineers, engineer sign-off, and price.

title: Hours Exchange: Supply Side of the Work Requirement
one_liner: Invert the wallet: instead of helping people prove hours they already work, build the network of pre-certified nonprofit and public hosts that supply verifiable, flexible community-service and training hours, with insured hosts and signed hour records, paid per active member-month by health systems and plans.
customer: First buyer: population-health, community-benefit and Medicaid-strategy leads at nonprofit and county-owned safety-net health systems. Second buyer: plans. Supply side: 20-50 hosts per county, such as food banks and church pantries, school after-care, libraries, senior centers, community gardens, and clinics' own non-clinical roles. Members: the residual slice of expansion adults who are not exempt, not already working and need hours.
problem: Every product in the parent's competitor set assumes the hours exist and only tracks or verifies them (SteadyIQ, Emmy, the state tracking portals from Maximus, Optum and Acentra, Pointcare, Findhelp). For a member who lost a job or has no hours, no amount of documentation fixes anything. The IFR does count community service, work programs and combined activities toward the 80 hours a month, but there is no supply chain: hosts do not know the state verification standard, cannot supervise flexible 4-hour shifts, lack liability cover, and have no time to produce signed logs. A member 30 days from termination cannot find, book and verify 40 missing hours on their own.
solution: An activity marketplace with a verification rail. (1) Host certification: each host signs a one-page state-format verification protocol (who may sign, what is recorded, non-displacement pledge) and joins a registry that we pre-clear with the state Medicaid agency wherever possible. (2) Micro-shift board: hosts post 3-6 hour shifts (pantry Saturday 8-12), and members claim them by SMS in their language. (3) Verification: check-in and out by phone geofence or supervisor QR or SMS confirmation, producing tamper-evident hour records. (4) Monthly hours letter in the state's format, delivered to the member, the case file and the plan. (5) Master volunteer accident and liability policy plus background checks carried by us, which is the small balance-sheet element and a reason hosts join. (6) Guardrails: the flow starts with an exemption and already-compliant screen, so nobody who qualifies is routed to slots. Participation is voluntary. Later: the same hours count toward SNAP's parallel 80-hour rule (widened by the 2025 law; verify scope), TANF work participation, and court-ordered or scholarship service hours.
why_now: The requirement starts Jan 1, 2027, but the documentation phase is later (an HFMA summary of the IFR says self-attestation is allowed through 2027 and once per beneficiary in 2028). That makes 2027 the year to build the host registry and get states to accept it, before the paperwork wall. The first wave of notices will expose the supply gap, and first movers will hold the hosts and the state relationships. Health systems and plans need a measurable coverage-retention lever for community-benefit and health-related-social-needs spending. Cheap SMS, geofencing and LLM-drafted state-format letters make per-shift verification nearly free.

title: Renewal Radar for Silent AI Exclusions
one_liner: Track carriers' filed AI exclusions and tell brokers, 90 days before renewal, which clients just lost AI coverage, then place the affirmative buy-back.
customer: Independent agencies and regional brokers (10-200 staff) with commercial books, their E&O carriers, and MGAs.
problem: Since January 2026 ISO-style generative-AI endorsements (CG 40 47 and CG 40 48) and far broader carrier forms, such as W. R. Berkley's 'absolute' AI exclusion, are attached at renewal, often buried. Clients use AI in ways they never disclosed. Brokers carry E&O exposure for failing to warn, and no tool maps which of a broker's 300 clients face AI exclusions or what AI each client actually uses.
solution: A rate and form filing scraper (public SERFF filing access) plus an endorsement parser that normalises exclusion breadth: gen-AI only versus any AI, bodily injury versus advertising injury, vendor-supplied AI. It feeds a renewal calendar imported from agency-management CSVs. A 12-question client AI-use questionnaire, optionally backed by an SSO or expense-report scan for AI tools. Output is a one-page 'AI coverage gap letter' plus a list of affirmative AI markets for placement.
why_now: 1 Jan 2027 renewals are the first big cycle after the Verisk endorsements became available, and AIG, Great American and Berkley filings landed through 2026. Affirmative AI capacity now exists (Armilla via Lloyd's, AIUC, Munich Re aiSure), so a gap and its fix can be sold together.
revenue_model: $250-800 per month per agency, $150-600 per gap letter for non-subscribers, 10-15% commission on affirmative cover placed, and $2-5k per month filing-intelligence subscriptions for MGAs and carriers.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is triggered by their own E&O fear, not curiosity about AI. The filings are public but unreadable, so the moat is a normalised exclusion database nobody at a brokerage has time to build. Silent AI cuts both ways: an unexcluded policy is a reason to ask for affirmative cover, so the gap letter also works as a sales tool for the broker.

title: Contingency Recovery of Missed Rotable Repair Warranties
one_liner: A success-fee auditor that finds repaired aircraft components that failed inside the shop's warranty window, and turns them into filed claims and cash.
customer: Small and mid-size operators with their own stores and a thin materials team. That means regional airlines, Part 135 cargo feeders and air-ambulance fleets, and Part 145 shops that buy their own exchange units. They pay 20-25% of whatever cash or credit is recovered, and nothing up front.
problem: A repaired starter-generator, bleed valve, hydraulic pump or fuel control that fails 4 months after the shop visit is often covered by warranty. Almost nobody claims it. The tech pulling the unit at 3 AM is trying to make a 6 AM departure and never sees the warranty terms. The repair invoice sits in accounts payable as a PDF. The removal record sits in the maintenance system, and hours and cycles sit in a third place. One materials coordinator owns thousands of removals a year, with 30-90 day claim windows. Three other leaks go unclaimed as well: 'no fault found' evaluation fees on units that were still under warranty, unreturned exchange cores that turn into penalty charges, and repair turnaround-time guarantees that shops never credit because nobody compares PO date to receipt date.
solution: Ingest three exports: removals and installs, PO and repair invoices (PDFs read with an LLM extractor), and the negotiated warranty terms. Match by part number and serial number, including interchangeable P/Ns. Flag every in-warranty failure, late repair turn, disputable NFF fee and open core. Then draft the claim on each vendor's own template, track it to a paid credit, and re-run monthly. Add a 3 AM 'is this unit under warranty?' lookup for maintenance control, so the claim gets started at the moment of removal.
why_now: Airline cost pressure on regionals is high, and mechanic wages rose sharply in 2024-2026, so labor cost per removal is up. Materials teams are being cut while fleets stay old. LLM invoice and PDF extraction only became reliable and cheap enough in the last 18 months, and that is the missing link, because the money sits in unstructured AP documents that MRO software never reads.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 20-25% of recovered cash and credits, with a 12-month tail on the audit. Later add a $2-5k per month SaaS tier for continuous monitoring, and sell benchmark data on shop warranty behavior to airline procurement teams.
non_obvious_insight: The leak is not in the maintenance system, it is in accounts payable. The tech who removes the part, the coordinator who could file the claim and the department that paid the invoice never share a screen. MRO software vendors will not fix it because warranty terms live in negotiated PDFs, not fields. Repair shops know most eligible claims are never filed, and they price that into their rates. A contingency auditor is the same playbook as freight-audit and telecom-audit firms, aimed at a niche nobody has covered.
first_30_days: Pitch 10 directors of maintenance and materials managers at small regionals, cargo feeders and helicopter EMS operators. Offer a free 12-month leakage audit, and ask them for the three exports. Build the matcher in Python plus an LLM invoice parser, and use a retired warranty or materials coordinator as a paid advisor for vendor quirks. Deliver a ranked claim list to the first 2-3 customers, file the claims yourself, and sign the success-fee agreement on the first credit memo. Publish the aggregate audit finding, such as the percentage of eligible failures that were never claimed, as the lead magnet.

title: Holdout Ledger: Landowner-Side Assembly Intelligence
one_liner: The landowner's half of the courthouse tape. It shows farm families and heirs in an assembly corridor who is buying around them, how close the buyer is to finishing, and how much leverage the last holdouts have, paid on closing.
customer: Owners of 100-2,000 acres in counties where recorded options and easements cluster, reached through ag and land-use attorneys, county farm bureaus, rural lenders and direct mail. Wedge: heirs, tenants-in-common and absentee owners who get anonymous offers under NDA. The payer is the landowner, on a contingent fee, plus subscribing law firms.
problem: Each landowner is approached alone by a landman working for an anonymous LLC. NDAs stop neighbors comparing notes. The developer sees the whole assembly and the owner sees one offer. Owners sign early and cheap, or hold out blindly, and cannot tell whether their parcel is a keystone or an afterthought. Landmen work for the buyer, local lawyers rarely have county-wide data, and county officials learn of the project from a leaked story.
solution:
1. 'Neighbor Check': enter a parcel or address and get a map of recorded instruments within about 5 miles, classified from the image. It shows the LLC family behind them, the share of the plausible footprint already recorded, whether the parcel sits on a critical path (contiguity, road access, a line crossing), expiring options, and a plain-English read of what the pattern usually means.
2. Owners in a cluster can opt into a negotiating pool, like the mineral-owner associations in oil and gas leasing. A licensed land broker or attorney partner represents them. We supply the analytics and take a success fee on closing.
3. We sell a group map subscription to ag and land-use law firms and farm-bureau chapters.
why_now: The 2025-26 large-load land rush has put anonymous NDA'd offers in front of thousands of rural owners, and local fights over data center land deals are widely reported. Owners can now see the buyer's footprint because public recorded memoranda can be read at scale with LLM vision. FinCEN's exemption for domestic companies means owners cannot ask who is behind the LLC and get a federal answer, so primary records are the only route. Reported prices such as roughly $100k an acre offered near Hill County, Texas, make the information gap worth real money to owners.
revenue_model: Free lookup as lead generation. $149-$399 for a full parcel report. A contingent success fee of 1.5%-3% of total consideration at closing, collected through a licensed broker affiliate. Example: a 300-acre owner closing a $4M option-plus-lease package yields $60k-$120k. $300-$800 a month per law firm or farm-bureau seat. Ten closed deals in year one is roughly $500k-$1M, at very low marginal cost after the data pull.
non_obvious_insight: The developer's own recorded memoranda reveal how complete the assembly is, and holdout value peaks in the last 20-30% of parcels. That is the moment owners are least informed. Every existing vendor's paying customer is the developer, so none can serve the counterparty without alienating buyers. That is counter-positioning in Helmer's sense. Landowners are numerous, each needs the service once, and assessor rolls are public, so mail reaches them cheaply. The demand is one-shot and high-stakes, which suits a contingent fee better than SaaS. The data burden is also small: a few dozen instruments per cluster, pulled per parcel, with none of the statewide bulk-ingestion risk.
first_30_days: Pick one county with a visible assembly. The parent's method of pulling 24 months of instruments gives the pattern. Mail 400 landowners within the cluster a letter with a QR code: 'Three LLCs using the same law firm recorded options on X acres within 4 miles of your land.' Offer a free Neighbor Check, then a $199 report. Sign a referral and co-marketing agreement with one licensed land broker and one ag attorney. Get 5 owners into a pooled negotiation and 20 paid reports. Before launch, have counsel confirm the broker-licensing and fee-sharing rules in the state (lawyers generally cannot split fees with non-lawyers), and use only public records. We are never a party to any NDA.

title: Immune-Graded Beef-on-Dairy Calves With Warranty
one_liner: A $1 refractometer reading at day 3-5 predicts whether a $1,400 crossbred calf lives, yet nobody independently verifies it at sale. Own that measurement and the warranty that follows.
customer: Calf raisers, backgrounders and feeder buyers who pay a premium for graded calves (or a subscription for the data), and dairies who pay to have calves graded so they can earn the premium. Later, insurers and MGAs underwriting a mortality warranty.
problem: Beef-on-dairy calf output went from about 50,000 head in 2014 to roughly 3.2M in 2024, with CattleFax projecting 5-6M, and calves have sold as high as $1,500 per head. Calf raisers buy 3-5 day old calves nearly blind and eat the 10-25% loss to scours and pneumonia. The colostrum information stays on the dairy, so raisers blame 'bad calves' and dairies blame 'bad luck'. Each dead calf now leaves a four-figure hole in a heifer pipeline that is short by hundreds of thousands of head.
solution: Independent serum total protein (Brix) testing on every calf at day 3-5, done at the dairy or at pickup by trained techs with digital refractometers and a phone app. Each calf is graded on the published four-tier passive-transfer scale (Excellent, Good, Fair, Poor) and logged with dairy, sire, weight and hydration score, then gets a QR tag or passport that follows the calf to the buyer. Buyers pay a premium for Excellent and Good and discount Poor. Phase 2 uses the accumulated data to price a 30- or 60-day mortality warranty ('we have graded 300,000 calves and know what a Brix 8.4 calf from Dairy X does'). Phase 3 gives dairies a colostrum scorecard that brokers use.
why_now: Crossbred calves are at record values, beef-on-dairy volume is doubling, and the heifer shortage means every lost calf is expensive and hard to replace. Consensus passive-transfer grading standards were published in 2020, digital refractometers are cheap, and buyers are already paying for verified genetics programs, so 'verified immunity' is the obvious next tag that nobody sells.
revenue_model: $4-6 per calf grading fee paid by the seller or split with the buyer, then $10-25 per calf warranty premium once loss data supports underwriting (partner with an insurer or MGA rather than carrying risk), plus a data subscription for larger calf raisers and feedlots.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone argues about sire genetics while the vet knows immune status dominates early death, and calves with failure of passive transfer carry about twice the risk of illness and death. The test is $1 and 60 seconds, but a number only has value when a neutral third party holds custody of it at the point of sale. The business is independent custody of the measurement, not the refractometer, and the resulting dataset becomes the underwriting moat.
first_30_days: Two vet techs, two $150 digital refractometers and a phone form. Offer free grading on 5 dairies' weekly calf shipments to 2-3 calf raisers or brokers. Ask the raiser to report 30-day illness and death by calf tag. After about 60 days, publish graded-versus-ungraded outcomes, then get one raiser to commit to a premium (for example $30-50) for Excellent calves and a discount for Poor, and charge the test fee from that point on.
