competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Where Food Comes From (third-party verification: Age Verification, Source Verification, USDA Process Verified Program, custom Process Verified claims), Calftech Corporation (Central Valley, CA calf ranch). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I could not run the planned searches on Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or vendor names. The 'nobody does this' finding therefore rests on direct page fetches and a GitHub repository search, not full web coverage. My early attempts to pull search-engine result pages through WebFetch returned junk or CAPTCHAs, and I stopped them because they sidestep the search limit. The verdict is low-to-moderate confidence.

What I found:
- No company selling per-calf independent Brix or serum total protein grading with a QR passport, and no calf-immunity warranty product. Where Food Comes From has no such program. Vytelle's site lists no calf program. GitHub has no relevant open-source tool, only hobby repos.
- Livestock Risk Protection explicitly 'does not protect against mortality, condemnation, physical damage or disease' (https://agproud.com/articles/60060-knowledge-is-the-best-insurance-an-overview-of-livestock-risk-protection). Federal cover for calf death loss is therefore absent. I did not verify what private mortality insurance exists.

What still stands in the way, and is not competition in the strict sense:
1. Self-testing. A raiser can Brix-test at arrival for about $1, and dairies can test their own calves. Independent custody only earns money where seller and buyer distrust each other's numbers, or where price is set before arrival.
2. Bilateral history. Feeders already ask which dairy the calves came from and some supply sire straws to dairies (https://agproud.com/articles/53106-factors-to-consider-before-buying-crossbred-dairy-beef-calves). Source-dairy reputation substitutes for per-calf grading.
3. Warranty moral hazard. Immunity is one driver of loss, but raiser housing, feeding and biosecurity dominate, which makes underwriting hard. Lombard's consensus paper puts failure of passive transfer at roughly twice the risk, which is a useful signal but not a full loss model.
4. Incumbents can absorb it. Verifiers, diagnostics vendors, calf-ranch networks and packer programs could add an immunity field.

Genuinely unserved: an independent, per-calf immunity record that travels from dairy to raiser to feeder to packer, plus a neutral dispute-resolution measurement.

title: Search-Fund Accelerator for Buying Scrap Yards
one_liner: A cohort program that turns laid-off mid-career managers into owner-operators of small scrap yards, e-scrap shops and transfer stations. It brings deal sourcing, environmental diligence and SBA-lender access.

Their storage and processing permits take years to obtain, and domestic scrap has just become strategic: the Aug 27, 2026 BIS rule forces black mass and tungsten scrap sellers to allocate 100% of sales to US buyers. Nobody packages this asset class for a first-time buyer.

Provide a standard diligence pack covering environmental liabilities and Phase I/II, fire history and insurance, permit transferability, commodity exposure and offtake contracts. Add a 90-day operator bootcamp with a mentor operator and introductions to SBA lenders. Take a fixed fee at close plus a small advisory equity stake.

Greenfield battery and plastics recycling is capital-destroying (Ascend Elements and Li-Cycle bankruptcies, 7 of about 30 US PET reclaimers closed), while boring, permitted, cash-flowing yards look safer. DoD and DOE equity stakes and the BIS allocation rule are re-rating domestic scrap.
revenue_model: Cohort tuition (about $4-6K per seat). Buy-side success fee ($25-50K or 1.5-2% at close). 2-5% advisory equity in each acquisition. Sell-side listing fees from retiring owners. Diligence-pack licensing to lenders.

title: Scribe-Adjusted EBITDA: Privileged Diligence for Physician Deals

The engaging party is the buyer's healthcare transactions counsel, so the work is privileged. Quality-of-earnings accounting firms are channel partners, not rivals.
problem: Buyers pay a multiple of EBITDA that now includes scribe-era E/M uplift, and drift dollars fall through at near-100% margin. Illustration (assumptions to validate): $30M revenue, 40% E/M, 6% scribe uplift gives $0.72M, about 14% of a $5M EBITDA, or roughly $8M of enterprise value at 11x. A stock deal also inherits overpayment liability, and the 60-day return rule starts once a problem is identified. Nobody in the deal team can answer the question. QoE accountants have no coder bench. Regulatory counsel runs generic billing samples. Seller materials and scribe vendor 'AAPC-verified' claims are self-serving. The parent's own research flags that the drift may be legitimate documentation catch-up, so buyers cannot tell whether to discount it or trust it.
solution: Deliverable is a 'Scribe-Adjusted Run-Rate Report', engaged through deal counsel under a privilege-preserving engagement letter. (1) Causal drift estimate: 24-36 months of claims from the data room plus each provider's scribe go-live date from the seller's admin console. Because rollouts are staggered, non-adopters and late adopters in the same group form a built-in control group, so a staggered difference-in-differences replaces a naive before/after. (2) Coder-signed sample: 150-300 stratified encounters from the highest-drift providers, reviewed by certified coders on MDM and time statements. This splits drift into 'supported catch-up' and 'at-risk narration'. (3) Outputs: a scribe-adjusted EBITDA range, an extrapolated overpayment exposure with a confidence interval, and recommended escrow, specific indemnity or price adjustment language. It also includes a 100-day post-close remediation and refund plan. (4) Later: the same report sold sell-side ('prove your uplift is clean before you go to market') to cut re-trades.
why_now: Scribes went mainstream across groups in 2025-26, so the first wave of PE deals with 12-24 months of scribe-era claims is closing now. Payers have begun automated E/M downcoding (Cigna's nationwide policy from October 2025 is reported), so uplift in the trailing run-rate may not persist. The FCA enforcement climate makes successor liability a live diligence topic. There is no historical playbook, because this diligence item did not exist in 2023.
revenue_model: $20-45k per buy-side report, priced by provider count and data volume. $8-15k for a sell-side readiness version. Optional 100-day post-close monitor at $4-8k per month. Direct cost is roughly $3-5k per report (30-45 coder hours plus senior review), so gross margin is about 80%. Two people can deliver one to two reports a week. A benchmark subscription for funds is a later add-on.
non_obvious_insight: Two things. First, the buyer does not need the scribe to be wrong. They need a number, and the staggered rollout gives each target its own control group, which the drift studies with pre/post design and the free-diagnostic framing in the parent both miss. Second, EBITDA leverage makes a $30k report protect about $8M of price, so it is priced against the deal, not against a compliance budget. The same report is also valuable to a seller with clean documentation, which makes it a two-sided product that gets better as deals accumulate.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build a public-data pre-screen from the CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service file (updated May 2026). It shows each NPI's E/M level mix by year for any target roster. Public data means no client claims and no privilege problem, but the year lag means it only catches early adopters, so the full report needs data-room claims. Retain a healthcare regulatory attorney to draft the privileged engagement template, and contract 2 CPC/CPMA coders. Days 8-30: contact 25 healthcare-transactions lawyers at mid-market firms and 20 lower-middle-market PE healthcare associates, offering a free public-data pre-screen on any target they are bidding on under NDA. Aim for one paid confirmatory-diligence pilot at $12-15k, in exchange for the right to keep de-identified aggregate statistics and a reference.

title: Revenue-Integrity Diligence for Water System Acquirers
one_liner: The buyer of a small or mid-size water system pays for a 10-day, account-level scan of the target's billing, meters and parcels. It prices hidden revenue and revenue-quality risk before signing, then a success fee on prospectively recovered revenue funds the first-100-days fix.
customer: Corporate development and integration leads at serial acquirers of municipal and small private water and wastewater systems. These are the acquisition teams of investor-owned utilities, PE- and infrastructure-fund-backed water platforms, contract operators bidding O&M or concession deals with revenue share, and regional authorities absorbing failing systems. Deal size is systems with 3k-60k connections.
problem: Buyers price municipal systems on reported revenue and customer counts. Their diligence covers engineering condition, financial audit and legal. Nobody tests account-level billing integrity beyond sampling a few bills. Sellers cannot fix leakage themselves: correcting a meter class, adding unbilled connections or raising a billing floor is politically radioactive for a council, and back-billing is legally capped. So the leakage stays buried until after close. The buyer then discovers it over years, after the price is set, so the buyer neither benefits from knowing it at pricing time nor budgets capex against it. The same blind spot hides negative surprises: estimated reads, stopped meters, dead accounts and customer counts that overstate the base.
solution: Ask the seller's data room for a standard extract: account list, 24-36 months of consumption, meter inventory, rate class and tariff, receivables aging. Join it to the assessor roll, building footprints, permits and public filings. Produce a Revenue Integrity Report in 10 days: (1) a parcels-with-structures versus billed-connections gap by service area; (2) a large-meter low-flow fingerprint ranking accounts by expected annual dollars; (3) read-quality and zero-read audit (estimated reads, stopped meters); (4) misclassified rate class or meter size; (5) a downside adjustment to the revenue baseline; (6) a 100-day plan with a prospective-only fix, a meter test and replacement list, and a price-adjustment memo for negotiations. After close, execute the plan with the buyer's CIS and the field-test subcontractor, and later normalize billing data across the buyer's whole portfolio.
why_now: PFAS, lead-line and aging-pipe capex plus affordability politics push small municipal owners toward selling or regionalizing. Serial acquirers and infrastructure funds are actively rolling up water systems. Fair-market-value sale statutes (for example Pennsylvania's Act 12) have made municipal sales a repeatable process. Diligence windows are short (30-60 days of exclusivity), which fits a 10-day data product. Open footprint data, interval data and LLM-assisted cleaning of messy municipal billing exports make a 10-day turnaround possible for two people.
revenue_model: Fixed diligence fee of $35-75k per target, paid from the deal budget and owed even if the buyer walks. Success fee of 15-20% of verified incremental billed revenue over 24 months post-close (prospective only, verifiable in the buyer's own CIS). Optional 100-day revenue plan retainer of $15k a month. Then a portfolio SaaS tier for serial acquirers: $3-6k per system per year for cross-system revenue-integrity monitoring. Bottom-up assumption: 30-60 diligence engagements a year at about $50k is $1.5-3M of revenue for a small team.
non_obvious_insight: The same $1 of recurring recovered revenue is worth about $1 a year in a city budget, but roughly 8-15x that to an acquirer valuing the system on earnings, and the buyer can bill correctly on day one. Change of ownership is the only moment when meter-class and connection corrections carry no council optics and no back-billing exposure. Payer and problem-owner are misaligned in the parent idea (the city pays for a fight it does not want). Moving the buyer of the utility into the payer seat removes procurement, contingency-ban and optics risk in one step. It also works as an option-free downside screen, which a buyer values on every deal, not only the rich ones.
first_30_days: Build a list of about 40 acquirers from state PUC acquisition dockets, fair-market-value sale filings and municipal sale RFPs. Pick three live or recently announced sale processes. Run a free public-data teaser for each: assessor parcels with structures inside the service area versus service connections in SDWIS and PUC filings, plus the top customers in the seller's annual financial report. Send two-page teasers to corporate development heads. Recruit one advisor, either ex-corporate development at a water utility platform or a water-M&A deal lawyer, for warm intros. Offer a half-price pilot diligence ($15-20k) on one live deal with a data-room extract. Confirm buyers' NDAs allow use of aggregated, anonymized yield data.

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Itron (Temetra Analysis / Non-Revenue Water portfolio), Badger Meter (BEACON, OneNetwork), Master Meter (Harmony Encore MDM), Metron-Farnier (WaterScope). Treat 'no direct competitor found' as unconfirmed, and do a manual pass on Crunchbase, YC and RFP portals before committing. What I did verify: (1) I found no vendor selling a contingency-fee service that joins assessor roll, footprints, imagery and the billing system to produce named unbilled addresses for water utilities. (2) The metering and analytics incumbents (Itron, Badger, Master Meter, Metron) sell software tied to their own hardware, with no evidence of a ranked, dollar-denominated, legal-ready recovery list or contingency pricing. Ghost-parcel discovery is the weaker half. A structure with no account is rare where permits trigger taps, and an ADU on a shared meter is usually already billed on consumption. Back-billing is politically and legally messy, and some jurisdictions restrict contingency contracts. Ameresco-style ESCOs sell projects after ownership is settled. Rate and valuation consultancies (Raftelis, FCS, Hazen and peers) are often on the seller side or the municipality's side, and they use sampled tests rather than account-level joins, which makes a buyer-side, conflict-free diligence product counter-positioned against them. There is no public procurement and no contingency-contract exposure, because the payer is a private acquirer.

title: Stack-Pooled 24/7 Article 14 Desk for Non-EU Brands
one_liner: A guaranteed-SLA Assigned Representative that files CRA Article 14 reports for 50-250 person non-EU connected-device brands, doing the triage once per shared component stack (Tuya, ESP-IDF, OpenWrt/Realtek) and fanning it out to every client on that stack.
customer: Medium-sized (50-250 staff, above the small-enterprise fine exemption) non-EU smart-home, e-mobility and networking brands based in Shenzhen, Taiwan, Korea and the US that sell into the EU via Amazon EU and retail. Their firmware comes from an ODM on one of 3 shared stacks: Tuya/Matter modules, ESP-IDF/ESP32, or OpenWrt/Realtek SDKs. The buyer is the head of product or compliance; the introduction comes through the EU Responsible Person/EPR (WEEE and packaging) service providers who already serve these sellers.
problem: These brands do not know what is inside their own firmware because the ODM built it, so they cannot tell whether a KEV/EUVD entry hits them. They have no one awake in Europe at 3am Sunday to decide 'actively exploited, affects us, file'. The 72h and 14-day clocks carry fines even if the 24h clock does not, and their EU retail partners will start asking for proof of process. Existing options each miss part of this. Software (CVD Portal, CRACI, Regulus) stops at timers and drafts, with filing left to the customer. Finite State and H-X draft notices but leave filing to the customer. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 or price. EcoComply is an AR mandate with no triage.
solution: Three things in one contract. (1) Named-analyst AR mandate plus a written SLA: triage decision within 4h and early warning filed inside 24h, weekends included, under a client-approved decision tree and pre-authorised actions. (2) Stack-pooled triage: a stack owner analyses each exploited entry once against the stack's component graph and issues per-firmware-version pre-approved VEX and notice drafts to every enrolled brand on that stack, so a client-named analyst only checks the version delta and files. (3) Firmware-fingerprint onboarding: the brand uploads a firmware image or OTA URL and the desk builds the component list itself, removing the missing-SBOM problem. Every KEV/EUVD entry also gets a timestamped per-product 'affected / not affected' decision, delivered monthly as a signed monitoring evidence log. That log is the recurring deliverable when nothing was exploited, and it is what retailers and market surveillance authorities will ask for. The 24h and 72h drills run on the client's own stack.
why_now: Article 14 reporting went live on 11 Sep 2026 (about 18 days ago) and the ENISA SRP opened the same day. Patchstack shows managed filing is now legal and being productised, so the window before it becomes a checkbox is roughly 6-12 months. Retail supplier manuals are being rewritten for the Dec 2027 full application, and GPSR (since Dec 2024) already trained these sellers to buy EU-representative services.
revenue_model: Base fee of about EUR 3.6-4.8k per year per product family (AR mandate, stack monitoring, monthly evidence log, one drill), well above EcoComply's EUR 1.5k AR-only anchor but below a monthly PSIRT retainer. Filing events cost EUR 1.5-3k each. Tabletop drills and 'clock audit' are EUR 1.5-5k. Wholesale white-label 24/7 back-end capacity is sold to TUV, DEKRA, Bureau Veritas, TridentSec and SBOM platforms. Target is 100 product families by month 12 (about EUR 400k ARR). One stack analyst covering 30-100 clients keeps gross margin above 65%.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not filing, it is the stack-to-firmware truth table. Brands do not know what is inside, but the desk sees which SDK forks and versions actually ship across dozens of brands. That is a cornered resource that a one-off consultancy cannot copy: each new client on a stack has near-zero marginal analyst cost and improves the fingerprint coverage. Also, 95% of what the desk produces is 'not affected'. Selling signed negative evidence as the monthly deliverable fixes the judges' 'insurance nobody buys until audited' flaw. Targeting 50-250 person firms sidesteps the Art 64(10) small-enterprise exemption on the 24h fine.
first_30_days: Week 1: get a professional-indemnity quote, and get written confirmation from ENISA or a national CSIRT that an external firm can serve as AR using personal EU Login accounts. Get counsel to settle how the 24h clock starts when the desk detects first, and draft the AR mandate and decision tree. Weeks 1-2: build component graphs for 3 stacks (ESP-IDF, OpenWrt/Realtek, Tuya) covering the top 25 exploited component families of the last 24 months, using open-source firmware unpacking such as EMBA. Weeks 2-4: sell a EUR 1.5k '24h drill + firmware fingerprint' to 20 brands sourced from 3 EPR/GPSR representative providers and Amazon-EU seller communities. The drill simulates an exploited entry hitting their stack and measures their real time-to-decision. Convert 5 into annual AR+desk contracts. Contract 3 part-time named analysts across time zones and confirm the SRP login rules apply to them.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TridentSec (PSIRT-as-a-Service), Finite State (managed CRA service), Cybellum (managed PSIRT / incident response service), Patchstack (managed CRA Article 14 reporting for open source). Cybellum's service targets enterprises. CVD Portal, CRA Evidence and other tools stop at timers and packages, and their final filing is a human step by the customer. Patchstack files as AR but only for open source, and free.

- The SBOM-to-CVE matching layer is commoditised. CVD Portal's Reporting tier is EUR 99/mo, and CRACI, Zealience, Regulus and ONEKEY sell the same thing.

It sells the one thing they call customer-owned, which is a contractually guaranteed filing as the named AR. It uses the SBOM and monitoring layer (CVD Portal at EUR 99/mo, CRACI, Zealience, ONEKEY) as commodity input rather than product. It is aimed at non-EU mid-size brands, which Cybellum's enterprise focus and Patchstack's free open-source-only service do not serve. Its economics come from pooling by stack, which per-client consultancies and per-seat platforms cannot match. Incumbent MSSPs and certification bodies (Kudelski, TUV SUD, DEKRA, Bureau Veritas) become white-label distributors rather than rivals, since the desk offers them the back end they lack.

title: Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure
one_liner: A daily feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements to show who is quietly assembling land for data centers, solar and transmission weeks before anyone announces it.
customer: Competing data center, solar, storage and transmission developers' land teams and site-selection consultants; utility and co-op large-load planners; infrastructure and energy funds buying alternative data; and county economic development and planning offices wanting defensive visibility.
problem: Land assembly is a race, and the first public trace is a short memorandum of option, lease or easement recorded at the county. Nobody watches those at scale. The assessor doesn't reflect an unexercised option. The clerk's document-type field is a dropdown chosen by a data-entry clerk, so big deals hide under 'Other', 'Miscellaneous' or 'Agreement'. Developers find out about a competitor's 6,000 acres months late, counties learn from a leaked newspaper story, and everyone pays landmen $300-$600 a day to sit in vaults.
solution: Ingest recorded instruments from county portals and bulk feeds in target corridors. Classify by reading the full image, not the clerk's label. Cluster by grantee, signatory, notary, return-to law firm and mailing address to unmask LLC families. Flag assembly events, such as N option memos within X miles or easement clusters along a line that imply transmission or pipeline. Deliver alerts, a map, and parcel-level chain-of-title and existing-easement packets on demand, with a human landman reviewing the hard ones.
why_now: The 2025-2026 large-load land rush is real: options in Hallam, Nebraska are reportedly worth tens of thousands of dollars an acre, and Hill County, Texas land appraised near $7,100 an acre has been offered about $100,000 an acre. Options are documented only by memoranda under NDA. FinCEN's 2025 decision to exempt domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. LLM vision finally reads messy scanned instruments accurately.
revenue_model: $2k-$8k/month per regional developer or utility seat, $750-$2,000 per tract title packet, and $50k-$150k/year alt-data licenses for funds. Optional revenue share or free access for counties that provide bulk feeds.
non_obvious_insight: The return-to address and notary on a recorded memorandum are the fingerprint of the developer's counsel, and they reveal an assembly weeks before a rezoning hearing. The mislabeled document-type field is why nobody has done this with generic data vendors. Landmen are the recorder's best regulars and know exactly which counties are hot, which makes them the cheapest ground-truth labelers and first customers.
first_30_days: Choose two counties with a rumored project, pull 24 months of instruments, and build the classifier and clustering. Deliver a 'who is assembling where' memo free to 10 site-selection consultants and land brokers, then convert two into $3k-$5k pilots. Check each state's bulk-data commercial-use rules and offer the counties access to the same maps.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ATTOM Data, Reonomy, Regrid, Enverus. White space: The specific product in the idea, a feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements from county recorders, classifies them from the image rather than the clerk's label, clusters LLC families by notary, return-to firm and address, and alerts on assembly patterns, was not found at any vendor I could read. Everything I could read is adjacent. Parcel and ownership vendors (Regrid, ATTOM, Reonomy) sell deeds, mortgages and LLC piercing but not options or easements. Siting and diligence vendors (Paces, Enverus, GridCARE) help a client find its own site. Project trackers (Cleanview, DC Byte, Heatmap Pro, Data Center Watch) start at permit or public news. Land-management vendors (Pandell, Enverus LandScape) manage a client's own documents. What remains open is cross-county, image-level reading of recorded non-deed instruments to detect other parties' assembly, sold as alerts. It is plausibly protected by the hard part, which is getting recorder access county by county, not the ML. The main structural doubts I could not test are whether developers actually record option memoranda before announcement, and how many counties allow bulk commercial pulls of document images.

title: Materials Capture Ratio: Pay-on-Lift for Flat-Rate Shops
one_liner: Measure what share of the parts a residential plumbing or HVAC shop buys actually reaches a customer invoice, coach the leak out tech by tech and job type, and charge 25% of the measured lift over a frozen baseline.
customer: Owner and office manager of residential plumbing and HVAC service-and-replacement shops with 8-25 trucks and $2-8M revenue. They run flat-rate pricing on Housecall Pro, FieldEdge or Jobber (or ServiceTitan without Procurement/AP) plus QuickBooks Online, and techs pull from truck stock restocked on account at Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply or a local house. First job types are water heater replacement and condenser/air-handler swaps, where the standard install kit is well defined (expansion tank, flex connectors, T&P valve, discharge pipe, gas flex, line set, disconnect, pad, whip). Reached through PHCC chapters and owner masterminds.
problem: The parent idea has three weak spots. (1) Retroactive found money is mostly uncollectible. A homeowner will not pay a $40 parts add-on six months after a completed job, so an audit that reports history overpromises. Real value is capturing correctly from now on. (2) Contingency on 'newly captured revenue' cannot be attributed, so owners will dispute the fee. (3) Ticket-to-job matching from emailed PDFs is messy because counter tickets carry a typed job name at best, and these shops have no PO-per-job discipline for a 3-way match. Meanwhile the recurring leak is real and habitual. Techs bill labor from the flat-rate book and forget the $6 valve, the wax ring or the whip, and nobody sees it because the two ledgers (supply-house spend and customer invoices) are never divided into each other.
solution: Lead with one owner-legible KPI, the Materials Capture Ratio (MCR): materials billed at cost divided by materials purchased at cost, by month, tech, job type and supplier. It is computed from two exports and needs no invoice-by-invoice matching. Read-only OAuth into QuickBooks Online pulls supply-house bills and restock POs. A CSV or API export from the field-service software supplies the invoice material lines. Day one output is 'of every $100 of parts you buy, you bill $X', per tech. Then learn the shop's own kit per top-10 flat-rate job type by parsing a sample of supply-house lines with an LLM, and each week send the office manager a missing-parts list: closed jobs whose invoice lacks items the kit says were bought, with the pricebook item ready to add, plus which are still rebillable (open T&M, commercial, home-warranty and maintenance-agreement jobs). Add a pre-invoice nudge in the tech's flow later. Supplier-side price drift, unclaimed return credits and repricing files are a free add-on from the same data, not the headline. Contract: freeze a 6-month baseline MCR from the export, then charge 25% of (MCR lift x purchases x the shop's own average materials markup) for 12 months, with the shop's accountant signing the baseline once. It converts to a $199-499 per month subscription that includes the peer MCR benchmark.
why_now: Tariff-driven list-price moves mean flat-rate pricebooks go stale in a quarter, so owners are already asking where margin went. LLMs make it cheap to learn a shop's per-job kit from messy supplier lines. QuickBooks Online and the field-service platforms now expose APIs and exports, so onboarding takes minutes rather than a consulting project. The 2025 copper, steel and aluminum tariff regime, per the parent's research, made materials cost the most volatile line in a service shop's P&L.
revenue_model: Year one is a pay-on-lift fee of 25% of measured incremental materials revenue over the frozen baseline (no lift, no fee), which pairs a low-risk sale with a clean way to dispute-proof attribution. Then a $199-499 per month monitoring and benchmark subscription. Illustration: a $4M shop that lifts capture by 1-2% of revenue recovers $40-80K a year and we earn $10-20K in year one. If the median shop's gap is under 0.5% of revenue, the hypothesis is falsified within 30 days.
non_obvious_insight: The asset is not the found dollars. It is the rate of capture, a ratio you can compute from two exports without matching one ticket to one job, which sidesteps the parsing problem and the retroactive-billing problem together. Pegging the fee to a pre-agreed baseline ratio makes the contingency indisputable, which the parent lacked. Level is not the point, since warranty parts, callbacks and inventory build legitimately lower MCR. What matters is the delta and the spread between techs on the same job type, and that spread turns a vague back-office audit into a coaching scoreboard the owner can act on Monday morning. Pooled over many shops, the per-job-type kit and the MCR distribution become the cornered data asset.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: recruit 8 shops from PHCC chapters and owner masterminds on Housecall Pro, Jobber or FieldEdge with QuickBooks Online. title: Widow-First Retention Drills for Wealth Advisors
one_liner: Sell independent advisors an annual 'if one of us dies' rehearsal for couples, because the defection risk sits at the first spouse's death, not with the kids.
customer: Independent RIAs and small wealth teams ($150M-$2B AUM) whose median client is 65+. The buyer is the firm principal or COO.
problem: The industry spends on next-gen events with heirs. Cerulli says about $54T of the transfer is spousal and about $40T of that goes to widowed women. The survivor is grieving, holds a house full of logins and unknown accounts, and has to decide whether to keep the advisor. Advisors are commonly said to lose most widows within a year (widely cited, verify). The cause is usually friction, not performance.
solution: A 90-minute 'Survivor Fire Drill' run by the advisor's team with a software kit. Each spouse's death is simulated in turn. The tool builds a First-90-Days playbook: who to call, which accounts exist, which autopays must keep running, and where the documents are. It audits titling and beneficiaries from the survivor's point of view and flags single points of failure, such as only one spouse knowing the passwords. It then schedules pre-agreed advisor check-ins at day 3, 14, 45 and 90. The advisor gets a dashboard of which couples have done the drill and where their exposure is.
why_now: Cerulli's Sept 2026 work frames retention of the transfer as the priority, and 89% of surveyed firms call family meetings essential. Wealth managers are buying heir-engagement tools, yet the first wave of money is spousal and the widow is under-served. Cheap document ingestion and secure vaults make the kit affordable for small firms.
revenue_model: $300-$700 per household per year billed to the firm, or a $25-40K/yr platform fee for a 100-household book. The ROI pitch: keeping one $1.5M widow at a 1% fee is worth $15K a year.
non_obvious_insight: The heir-retention narrative aims at the wrong person on the wrong day. Widows rarely leave over portfolio returns. They leave because nobody made the first 90 days easy. A rehearsal also works where estate planning fails, because people avoid 'planning' but will attend a scheduled drill.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-5 RIAs through advisor communities and podcasts. Run drills by hand with a spreadsheet and printed binder for each firm's 10 oldest couples. Record time-to-locate-accounts and the number of single-point-of-failure findings. Charge a $2.5K pilot fee and turn the findings into a retention case study the advisor can show prospects.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Empathy (LifeVault + Loss Support), Everplans (Enterprise / advisor channel), Trustworthy (Family Operating System), Wealth.com. White space: Nobody found sells the specific wedge: a facilitated, scheduled couples rehearsal of the first spouse's death, run by the advisor's team. That means simulating each spouse's death in turn with the surviving spouse actually doing the tasks; a survivor-point-of-view audit of titling, beneficiaries, autopays and password single points of failure; pre-agreed day 3/14/45/90 advisor check-ins; and a firm dashboard of drill completion and exposure. Vaults (Empathy, Everplans, Trustworthy) and estate-document platforms (Wealth.com, Vanilla) store information and generate documents, but their pages describe no behavioral ritual, no survivor-POV stress test and no post-death outreach cadence. Independent RIAs at $150M-$2B AUM are also not Empathy's core buyer (insurers, banks and big wealth firms). Caveats: I did not confirm that Empathy lacks scheduled outreach (its Connect page 404'd), and I could not check consultant-led widow-retention programs (see the note under evidence_of_demand). The software layer is commoditized (Trustworthy at $10 per client per year), so the defensible white space is the ritual, the audit method and the outreach cadence, not the vault.

title: China-Asset Diligence Desk for Pharma BD
one_liner: A bilingual scientist-plus-software sprint that verifies China-sourced drug packages (raw data, GLP and CMC standing, ownership chain) in 72 hours for US buyers.
customer: Pharma BD&L teams, NewCo-building VCs, royalty funds and mid-cap biotechs in-licensing Chinese assets.
problem: About one-third of 2025 licensing spend involved China-sourced drugs (Jefferies) and the pace accelerated in 2026 (Lilly-InnoCare up to $3.35B, Merck-SciBrunch $2.1B). Diligence infrastructure looks thin (inference): data packages are in Chinese formats, raw-data and audit-trail norms differ, and CRO and CDMO GLP or GMP standing is hard to verify. BIOSECURE, enacted Dec 18, 2025, requires OMB to publish the list of biotechnology companies of concern by December 2026 and FAR rules follow, adding an ownership and supply-chain axis.
solution: A fixed-price 'Asset Verification Sprint'. LLM-assisted translation and structured extraction of study reports. Bilingual scientists spot-check raw data and audit trails. Verify CRO and CDMO inspection histories (NMPA, FDA, EMA) and check ownership chains against the BIOSECURE lists. Deliver a Western-format gap analysis for IND-enabling needs (GLP tox acceptability, CMC comparability).
why_now: Deal flow is at record levels, BIOSECURE list publication is due in about three months, and biopharma layoffs (15,000+) free bilingual ex-pharma scientists.
revenue_model: $25-70k per sprint, $150-300k annual retainers for NewCo-builder VCs, and supply-chain mapping as a second product once the BIOSECURE lists land.
non_obvious_insight: The gap is not legal or financial diligence. It is data literacy and tacit standards, for example what counts as GLP-grade raw data, and Western deal associates cannot read the packages. The same team and database serve a second product, supply-chain mapping, when the lists arrive.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-4 bilingual ex-pharma scientists. Price a $20k pilot sprint. Approach 5 NewCo VC platforms and 5 mid-size pharma BD heads. Build a CRO and CDMO inspection database from public regulator records.

Stealth boutiques and Big-4 or CRO consulting units were not exhaustively checked.

title: Contributor-Only Delay Outcome Ledger for Immigration Solos
one_liner: A give-to-get ledger that joins public dockets with the USCIS action dates only the filing lawyer sees, sold as a triage score plus a consent-order-first filing pack for a solo's existing stuck files in the four highest-moot districts.
customer: Solo and 2-5 attorney immigration firms whose book is mostly naturalization, family-based, I-751 and I-765 work, already admitted in E.D.N.Y., D.N.J., D. Conn. or E.D. Mich. (the districts where Mandamus.com's own tally shows 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action). Narrowest wedge: a firm holding 10+ files already past posted times or more than 120 days past a naturalization interview. Those are existing paying clients, so each filing is a $2.5-5k upsell with zero acquisition cost. Secondary buyers later: boutique mandamus firms and litigation funders, as data licensees.
problem: Solos sit on stuck files and do not file, for reasons the judges and the competitor research surfaced. (1) They cannot tell which suits will be quietly mooted and which will draw a motion to dismiss: nationality-hold suits went 0-13 in D.D.C. this summer, and the Fifth Circuit bars I-485 delay claims (Cheejati). (2) They cannot price a flat fee without knowing the tail if the government fights. (3) A free pro se guide plus a $5,000 boutique make a $400 drafting tool look redundant, and general AI drafting is eroding the 6-10 hour learning curve. Public stats are hand-tallied for about 7 districts, and a docket shows when a case ended, not why or when USCIS actually acted.
solution: Three pieces, all attorney-of-record signed (the company is software). (1) Stuck-Case Book: paste or CSV-import pending cases from any case-management export (no partnership needed). It ranks each file by ripeness and expected days from service to USCIS action. Ripeness is tiered: N-400s more than 120 days after interview under 8 U.S.C. 1447(b), where the statute supplies the clock and in most circuits USCIS cannot adjudicate until the court remands, come first; then I-751, I-765 and long-idle I-130/I-140 under the APA. It refuses to generate filings for nationality-hold and Fifth Circuit I-485 cases and says why. (2) Filing pack: complaint, exhibits, service checklist, 60-day answer calendar, a documented pre-suit exhaustion checklist (e-request, Ombudsman, congressional inquiry) that also builds the 'not substantially justified' record, and a consent-order-first settlement template with an express EAJA reservation and a 30-day fee-petition reminder. (3) The ledger: after each case the attorney logs service date, USCIS action date and how it ended (consent order, quiet adjudication, MTD granted or denied). Judge- and AUSA-level detail unlocks only for contributors; everyone else gets a free coarse district scorecard.
why_now: The Oct 2025 end of the 540-day EAD auto-extension made I-765 delay suits a primary remedy, and holds keep files idle, but D.D.C.'s June-Aug 2026 record (government 13-0) means undifferentiated 'just file' now loses, so triage suddenly has value it lacked two years ago. LLM drafting has turned complaint templates into a commodity, pushing value to judgment and data. Honest caveat: RECAP counts look flat (385, 352, 477 filings a year in 2023-25), so the pitch is a higher win rate per filing, not a volume surge.
revenue_model: Free: coarse district scorecard (lead magnet and SEO). Paid: $299/month Ledger Pro (unlimited Stuck-Case Book, 2 filing packs a month, judge/AUSA-level data for contributors), extra packs $250 each. Flat fees only, never a share of the lawyer's fee. Year 2: data licenses ($1-3k/month) to boutique firms, litigation funders and case-management vendors. Bottom-up (assumptions to validate): about 1,500 target solos in the four districts x 20% penetration x about $3.6k/year is roughly $1.1M ARR before adding districts.
non_obvious_insight: A docket records when a suit ended, not when or why USCIS acted; stipulations and the 60-day answer clock add weeks of noise. The real key is service date, then USCIS action date, then dismissal type, and only the filing lawyer holds the approval notice. Every competing stat (Mandamus.com's hand tally, Lex Machina/Trellis-style docket analytics, raw CourtListener) is blind to it, so the moat is a cornered resource that accrues only through contributors and cannot be scraped. Second, the solo's blocking question is not 'can I draft this' but 'what does it cost me if the government fights'; tail probability by district is what lets them quote a confident flat fee.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: run the 8 real web searches the prior research could not (mandamus AI, delay-suit software, Crunchbase, AILA toolkits). Days 1-21: hand-label roughly 300 USCIS delay dockets from 2023-26 in E.D.N.Y., D.N.J., D. Conn. and E.D. Mich. from CourtListener/RECAP (cause of ending, days to end) and publish a free district scorecard. Days 7-30: pull the roughly 60 attorneys of record who file most of those suits (public) and offer free lifetime Founding Contributor status in exchange for backfilling 10 past cases with USCIS action dates from their approval notices; separately offer 100+ non-filing solos in the same districts a free 10-minute Stuck-Case Book audit of their own pending files and pre-sell 5 at $299/month. Go/no-go: 5 paying firms and 100+ outcomes with action dates logged by day 30.

Conn., DNJ and EDMI at 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action).

Parts of the pitch look weak against what I found:
(1) Nationality-hold suits look poor. Per Mandamus.com's summary of 13 D.D.C. delay decisions from June to August 2026, the government won all 13. Judge Leon in the consolidated Ivanov case found the categorical pause unexplained but dismissed the delay and mandamus counts under TRAC and limited relief to named plaintiffs. Docketwise has no litigation features; this rides on CSV export so it does not depend on it, and if Docketwise adds templates it still cannot copy a contributor-fed ledger. Lex Machina/Trellis and CourtListener see docket events only, not agency action dates or consent-versus-quiet outcomes; this builds on CourtListener rather than competing with it. title: Federal-Agreement Lab for State SNAP QC Reviewers
one_liner: Sell calibration drills to the small, high-leverage group whose findings set the official error rate, the state QC reviewers, scoring them against a federal answer key and putting part of the fee at risk on the state-federal disagreement rate.
customer: State SNAP Quality Control unit directors and the state SNAP directors who sponsor them, in the 41 states above 6% that must now file remediation plans. Each QC unit is a few dozen reviewers. Warm lead: Alabama DHR, which posted an RFP for 'SNAP Quality Control review assessment and training'. Check who won and at what scope. Targets: states within about 1 point of a tier line, once the FY2025 state table is pulled.
problem: The official rate is not the state's own number. USDA re-reviews a subsample and adjusts (regresses) the state's findings, and disputed differences go to arbitration. Rates are cliffs (6/8/10%), each worth tens to hundreds of millions in state benefit cost. A state QC reviewer who under-calls errors gets corrected upward by federal re-review. One who over-calls inflates the state's own rate. QC units are small and turnover-prone, and the FNS 310 handbook is dense. Today that calibration happens ad hoc, in meetings or through occasional consultants.
solution: A library of about 200 synthetic completed-review packets: case file, interview notes and an 'as-reviewed' finding, with planted misses and planted false alarms. Answer keys are adjudicated by retired FNS and state reviewers and cite FNS 310 sections. Reviewers find the errors, and we score agreement with the key by element (income, household composition, shelter, resources, ABAWD/H.R.1 rules), by reviewer and by supervisor. We add weekly live calibration sessions run by the retired reviewers, and an arbitration-readiness checklist. We do not perform QC reviews. We train and score, which keeps us clear of the federal oversight rules for third-party QC contractors (verify against the 2018 Farm Bill provisions). Method is symmetric: the goal is agreement with the federal standard, not lower error counts.
why_now: FY2025 rates came out June 24, 2026: 41 states above 6% and a 10.62% national rate. FY2026 rates finalize through federal re-review and arbitration into mid-2027, and states can use the better of FY2025 and FY2026 for FY2028. The FY2027 sample opens Oct 1, 2026 and sets FY2030 cost share. H.R.1 made every QC finding a budget line, so QC directors now have executive attention and remediation-plan deadlines. The Alabama RFP shows states already buy QC-side assessment and training.
revenue_model: $90-250k per state QC unit per year: about $2.5-4k per reviewer seat, a packet-library license and quarterly calibration sessions. 20-25% of the fee is at risk, refunded if the state-federal difference rate on FNS re-reviewed cases does not narrow. FNS measures that outcome, not us. 41 states at 40% penetration is about $5-8M ARR, so the ceiling is small but each logo is high-value and fast to close. Expansion: Medicaid eligibility-error programs (H.R.1 adds payment reductions starting around FY2030, verify), plus a per-case add-on for arbitration memo review. Prices are unvalidated assumptions.
non_obvious_insight: Dollars at stake per trained head is 100-1000x higher for QC reviewers than for eligibility workers. A 30-person unit's calibration can swing a tier cliff worth $100M+, and a county worker's cannot. The regressed rate turns under-calling into a hidden tax, not good luck. Unlike eligibility policy, which varies by state, QC review method is national (FNS 310), so one packet library serves every state. That fixes the parent's per-state case-library cost problem. The buyer population is tiny, homogeneous and reachable through a few networks.
first_30_days: Days 1-5: pull the Alabama RFP, announcement and results documents to learn the winner, scope and price. Recruit 2 retired state or FNS QC reviewers as adjudicators at $100-150 an hour. Days 5-18: write 25 planted-error packets from the public FNS 310 handbook and published arbitration guidance. Days 10-30: reach 15 QC directors through APHSA payment-accuracy contacts and FNS regional liaisons. Offer a free blind 10-packet test for 5 of their reviewers and return an agreement-gap report within a week. Convert 1-2 to $25-40k pilots via simplified procurement.
